items.title: How Price Shocks Moderate Pro‐Environmental Social Norms for Sustainable Consumption
items.abstract: Price inflation is a major and urgent consideration for consumers and governments around the world. This study measures how price shocks moderate pro‐environmental social norms and sustainable consumption. By combining the insights from a local survey on social norms and panel regression results from a large national survey, the study shows how price shocks in relation to energy, food, and water change social norms (descriptive and injunctive). The analysis also identifies a dynamic relationship between price and pro‐environmental social norm changes and their translation into behaviour. The new phenomenon not studied previously leads to the stipulation of ‘price norm theory’. Financial incentives via price change drive both a rational economic and a social norms response. This important and novel insight is relevant to understanding the influence of inflation and economic incentives on sustainable consumption. Policymakers can change pricing and financial incentives and influence social norms (in addition to consumer benefit–cost ratios).

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration and Sustainable Business Model Innovation with Platform Dependence
items.abstract: Digital platforms provide entrepreneurial firms with resources while constraining their strategic discretion. Drawing on paradox theory, this study examined associations between respondents’ human–AI collaboration (HAIC), paradoxical cognition (PC), ecosystem hybrid orchestration capability (EHOC), platform dependence (PD), and reported sustainable business model innovation (SBMI). We analysed 379 matched single-informant records collected in China in March and April 2026, with a mean interval of 23.92 days. The analysis used categorical controls, HC3 inference, formal shape tests, and 5000 bootstrap resamples. HAIC exhibits significant negative curvature in relation to SBMI, but the upper-bound slope test is borderline (one-sided p = 0.05002); the strict inverted U shape is therefore not robustly confirmed. The HAIC-squared term is not statistically significant in the executive subsample, and formal interaction tests do not establish a difference between respondent groups. The serial indirect association through PC and EHOC decreases between low and high HAIC, whereas the EHOC-only pathway increases, and the total indirect difference is not significant. PD negatively moderates the EHOC–SBMI association in the linear model; an exploratory quadratic specification reveals a more complex boundary. The findings distinguish cognitive and resource-coordination associations in a single-informant observational design.

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration and Value Co-Creation in Digital Ecosystems: A Theory-Driven Systematic Review and Research Agenda
items.abstract: Purpose: This review synthesizes evidence from recent studies of human–AI collaboration in service and digital ecosystems to build and test a multi-level conceptual framework. Design/methodology/approach: Thirteen studies (Tier A) from 2024 to 2026 were analyzed in full text and compared with 25 qualitative and mixed-methods studies (Tier B). In total, 38 service and digital ecosystem studies were analyzed within this review. Service-Dominant (S-D) Logic and the Affect–Behavior–Cognition (ABC) model was used as the underlying theoretical framework. Narrative and thematic analysis were employed to synthesize the results from the included studies. Findings: Transparency, process control and outcome control have significant effects on employees in terms of cognitive and behavioral effects, while system-initiated engagement has little effect. Human–AI interaction does not, on average, perform better than the best human in each task (g = ?0.23, p < .001), but does perform better than a single human in a variety of tasks (g = 0.64). Value is created through the integration of systems and not through technology itself. User experience, digital maturity, interoperable IT, and AI-induced technostress condition value realization. Originality/value: The study provides a three-stage framework, seven testable hypotheses, seven gaps in current research and an operational measurement for value creation at the employee level and for firm- and network-level value co-creation.

items.title: Human–AI risk decision-making: The effects of risk-taking tendency and transparency design
items.abstract: This study investigated how artificial intelligence (AI) risk-taking tendencies and transparency design influence human risk-taking behavior, trust in AI, and neural activity in risky decision-making contexts. Drawing on previous findings of human–AI collaboration and social influence, we examined human–AI interaction during the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART), using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to measure cerebral activation. The study employed a 2 × 2 between-subjects design (risk-taking vs. conservative AI; transparent vs. non-transparent design). A total of 120 participants completed the task under one of four experimental conditions. Behavioral results showed that participants initially increased their risk-taking behavior when paired with risk-taking AI, but gradually reverted to baseline, indicating increasing risk-aversion over time. Conservative AI did not significantly reduce risk-taking behavior below baseline, though it elicited higher trust ratings. Contrary to predictions, similarity in risk-taking tendency did not significantly enhance trust. Transparency design accelerated risk-aversion toward risk-taking AI and reduced trust bias toward conservative AI. Neuroimaging results revealed decreases in prefrontal and temporoparietal junction oxygenated hemoglobin, consistent with cognitive offloading when AI advice was present; these effects were attenuated under the transparent condition, suggesting sustained engagement. Overall, findings highlight the dynamic nature of human–AI risk decision-making and underscore the role of transparency in calibrating trust and maintaining user involvement in risky decision-making tasks.

items.title: Immersive simulation-based learning with virtual prototypes: advancing student engagement and educational quality in engineering
items.abstract: Purpose Immersive learning environments have been widely recognized for their potential to support student engagement in engineering education; however, their adoption is often constrained by high costs and limited accessibility. This study aims to examine the use of low-cost virtual prototypes as an alternative to high-cost immersive learning technologies in higher engineering education, with particular emphasis on accessibility and sustainability. Design/methodology/approach A one-group quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design was implemented with a sample of 92 undergraduate engineering students in a Latin American university context. Student engagement was assessed using a validated multidimensional instrument based on the Burch Engagement Survey for students framework, capturing physical, emotional and cognitive dimensions. Given the presence of both matched and unmatched observations, engagement differences were analyzed at the dimension level using statistical methods appropriate for partially overlapping samples, with effect sizes and confidence intervals reported to support interpretation. Findings The results showed pre–post increases in physical engagement and, to a lesser extent, emotional engagement after the intervention. In contrast, no statistically significant changes were found in synchronous or asynchronous cognitive engagement. These results suggest that virtual prototypes may be associated primarily with active participation, while deeper cognitive engagement may require additional scaffolding, reflection and metacognitive support. Originality/value This study contributes to the discussion of accessible engineering education by providing evidence on low-cost immersive tools and by identifying potential connections with sustainability-oriented educational goals. While the findings may align with goals of inclusion and equity in Sustainable Development Goal 4, they should be interpreted cautiously due to the study’s design. The results offer practical insights for technology-enhanced learning environments and future research directions.

items.title: Improving Explanations: Applying the Feature Understandability Scale for Cost-Sensitive Feature Selection
items.abstract: With the growing pervasiveness of artificial intelligence, the ability to explain the inferences made by machine learning models has become increasingly important. Numerous techniques for model explainability have been proposed, with natural-language textual explanations among the most widely used approaches. When applied to tabular data, these explanations typically draw on input features to justify a given inference. Consequently, a user’s ability to interpret the explanation depends on their understanding of the input features. To quantify this feature-level understanding, Rossberg et al. introduced the Feature Understandability Scale [ 49 ]. Building on that work, this proof-of-concept study collects understandability scores across two datasets, proposes a co-optimisation methodology of understandability and accuracy and presents the resulting explanations alongside the model accuracies. This work contributes to the body of knowledge on model interpretability by design. It is found that accuracy and understandability can be successfully co-optimised while maintaining high classification performances. The resulting explanations are considered more understandable at face value. Further research will aim to confirm these findings through user evaluation .

items.title: Influência da inteligência artificial nos processos cognitivos: atenção, memória e tomada de decisão
items.abstract: The progress of digital technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, has been transforming everyday life by acting as a support for cognitive processes such as attention, memory and decision making. With the growing use of technology and easy access to information, a change in human behavior can be noticed: instead of memorizing content, people prioritize quick access to it, which raises doubts about the effects on critical thinking and intellectual autonomy. Research such as that of Sparrow et al. (2011) suggests that the internet makes it easier to remember where to find information, rather than concentrating on retaining the content itself. Risko and Gilbert (2016) discuss cognitive "offloading" to technological devices, which may reduce mental effort. Simon's (1955) theory of bounded rationality helps to understand decisions made under cognitive limitations, a context in which AI can act as a support resource. Given this, the aim of this study is to analyze how artificial intelligence influences attention, memory and decision making, seeking to understand whether its use favors cognitive optimization or may cause negative long-term impacts. It is a qualitative, exploratory and descriptive literature review that gathered 21 works. The studies indicate that frequent and unreflective use of these tools may favor the transfer of cognitive tasks to external resources and excessive trust in AI responses, but the evidence on attention comes from digital technologies in general, and research on generative AI is still scarce and, to a large extent, preliminary. Better performance on a task done with AI does not, by itself, amount to learning.

items.title: Integrating AI Coding Agents Into Scientific Research
items.abstract: New software tools have emerged that enable AI agents to quickly develop code that analyzes data and generates figures, but their mistakes can also harm a researcher's computer, require extensive resources for validation, and cause the results to be received more skeptically. These concerns could be mitigated if scientific software is developed in a secure environment with a system for monitoring file changes and well-defined standards for handling AI agents. This paper first describes how coding agents change eleven aspects of generating, verifying, and reproducing numerical results. A six-level scale is then proposed for classifying AI-assisted numerical experiments by their provenance, reproducibility, openness, oversight, and falsifiability (PROOF). The scale begins with locally self-consistent, version-controlled, human-verified results and culminates in a publicly accessible and curated archive of the files, change history, prompt transcripts, independent agent regeneration of the analysis, and multiple cryptographically verifiable attestations of regeneration by independent researchers. These aspects of AI-assisted scientific software development have been synthesized into a new open source software package called vaibify that optimizes the agentic development of computational experiments ascending the PROOF Ladder. Docker containers sequester the agents while a GUI enables researchers to prompt command line agents, monitor the current status of local and remote files, and drive a project to PROOF Level 3 (reproducible). The methods described in this paper could help researchers reduce the time required to verify agent-written software and efficiently communicate trust in AI-assisted science.

items.title: International students and cross-cultural adaptation in China: A latent growth model of positive affectivity and relationship-building
items.abstract: The herein presented latent growth model, grounded in the integrative communication theory, examines how international students’ trait positive affectivity relates to cross-cultural adaptation through proactive general socializing and networking. A four-wave longitudinal study of 140 international undergraduate students in a Chinese university revealed that positive affectivity is positively related to psychological adaptation and negatively related to sociocultural adaptation difficulty, and that it predicts improvement in both outcomes over time. General socializing and networking showed distinct mediating roles in these relationships, with socializing explaining changes in psychological adaptation and networking explaining changes in sociocultural adaptation difficulty. By modeling adaptation trajectories with latent growth analysis and focusing on proactive relationship-building behaviors that expand access to social and informational resources, the study contributes to a more dynamic understanding of cross-cultural adaptation and suggests practical strategies for universities wanting to help international students adapt to new cultures.

items.title: Islamic Ethical Leadership and Employee Innovative Work Behavior in the AI Era
items.abstract: Universities are increasingly requiring their employees to be innovative, with a growing reliance on new digital tools, but it remains to be seen how innovation can be fostered by leaders demonstrating Islamic ethical values (justice, trustworthiness, consultation, truthfulness, and excellence) and whether the involvement of employees in the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace will make a difference. The present research involved 465 academic and administrative staff of public and private universities in eight cities of Pakistan. Based on social learning and social exchange theories, it mapped out the relationship between employees' perceptions of their leaders' behaviors and their perceptions of how safe they felt expressing unfinished ideas, and then how often they generated, championed, and implemented new ideas, and examined whether trust in the use of AI tools affected this process. A coherent picture began to emerge. Leaders who were described as fair, trustworthy, and consultative were seen to create a safe environment for others to share their ideas, and this created a small but strong influence on innovation; a direct leadership relationship still existed. Trust in AI was correlated with increased innovative behavior on its own, but did not obviously increase or decrease the relationship between psychological safety and innovative behavior; it seems that the two resources operated independently. The pattern was confirmed after adjusting for demographic factors and for institutions. Psychological safety then becomes a partial conduit for values-based leadership; AI trust becomes an additive but not a conditioning resource, but a single-source, single-time design can't establish causation.

items.title: Job Autonomy, Cognitive Load and Technology Adaptation Behaviour in Small and Medium Enterprises: A Moderated-Mediation Framework
items.abstract: Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in emerging economies are introducing digital tools faster than they are redesigning jobs around them. Job autonomy is the work design lever most often recommended for this transition, yet evidence on its effect on employees' technology adaptation behaviour is mixed. This conceptual paper integrates cognitive load theory with self-determination theory to explain why. It argues that autonomy supports technology adaptation through motivation but, beyond a certain level and under complex tasks, also raises the working-memory demands of learning new systems, so that cognitive load partially offsets its benefits. The paper proposes a moderated-mediation model in which cognitive load mediates the autonomy–adaptation relationship, task complexity shapes the autonomy–load link, and digital leadership acts as a boundary condition on both the direct and indirect paths: leaders who combine a learning orientation with clear structure are expected to lower the load that unstructured discretion creates. Generational cohort is treated as a proxy for prior digital experience rather than as a fixed trait. Six propositions, one of them in two parts, are derived and a survey-based research design for Vietnamese SMEs is specified, including measures, a two-wave data collection protocol and a partial least squares estimation strategy with quadratic and conditional indirect effects. The framework offers HRM researchers a testable account of when autonomy helps or hinders adaptation, and offers SME managers a rationale for calibrating autonomy and leader structure during technology roll-outs rather than maximising either.

items.title: Keeping humans in the loop: AI-assisted curriculum at program scale
items.abstract: As universities adopt generative AI for curriculum development, a central risk is that efficiency gains may come at the expense of educational judgement, disciplinary expertise and human connection. Yet the same technology, used selectively, can free academics to focus on how students think and solve problems (Truu, 2026). This poster presents a programmatic, human-led method for AI-assisted course development used across UNSW College’s new Applied Degrees: industry co-designed, work-blended bachelor programs in business and information technology. It addresses two questions: how can generative AI support curriculum development at program scale while preserving human educational judgement; and where must that judgement be structurally embedded? The method is grounded in constructive alignment (Biggs & Tang, 2011) and human-centred AI (Le Dinh et al., 2025), applied at program rather than course level. The main focus is programmatic coherence. Rather than building courses one at a time, the method applies shared design patterns across an entire program. Even with different subject matter experts (SMEs) and program leads contributing to different courses, these design principles remain consistent from first year to capstone. AI generates content within this architecture, but functions as a structured design assistant rather than an autonomous author. Different workflow stages route to different AI models suited to each context. This preserves checkpoints where human framing and contextual judgement re-enter the process, consistent with calls to keep human control central to AI in education (Alfredo et al., 2024; Bearman et al., 2023; Hau, 2025; Islam, 2026). The human-led, AI-supported workflow moves from industry and academic SME input and course overview revision through curriculum blueprinting, assessment critique, rubric development, Canvas-ready asynchronous content, workshop planning, and student-facing resources. The assessment-critique stage is especially significant as generative AI reshapes what assessment must do, with recent scoping evidence showing AI is driving a re-examination of assessment design across student, teacher and institutional levels (Chiu et al., 2024). Human judgement remains decisive throughout: SMEs establish disciplinary intent; program leads review coherence and progression; learning designers evaluate scaffolding, accessibility and learner experience; and final quality assurance confirms alignment before publication. The ASCILITE Technology Enhanced Learning Accreditation Standards (TELAS, 2022) informed the design from the outset and now provide the basis for review, making quality auditable. This matters for Applied Degrees, where quality depends on integrating academic standards, industry relevance, work-integrated learning and inclusive learning design. Outputs are structured for continuous improvement in Canvas, keeping pedagogical authority close to the point of delivery rather than locked inside opaque AI outputs (UNESCO, 2023). Critically, automating the repetitive build frees human effort for the work most often skipped under time pressure: the programmatic view, gathering student feedback, time with industry to collect current case studies and simulations, and targeted employability development so graduates are work ready. AI can accelerate curriculum production while strengthening human-centred design, provided the architecture and its checkpoints are designed first. The contribution is that architecture. The design patterns, curriculum blueprinting and checkpoints where human judgement re-enters are transferable to other program-scale builds regardless of which AI tools are used.

items.title: Latent profiles of artificial intelligence ethical awareness and their association with professional identity among nursing interns: A multicentre cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into nursing education and clinical practice, nursing interns need to recognise and address ethical issues associated with its use. However, heterogeneity in their AI ethical awareness remains poorly understood. This study aimed to identify latent profiles of AI ethical awareness among nursing interns, examine factors associated with profile membership, and compare professional identity across profiles. Methods: A multicentre cross-sectional study was conducted among 550 nursing interns from 12 hospitals in China between September and October 2026. Data were collected on sociodemographic characteristics, AI ethical awareness, attitudes towards AI use in nursing, ethical sensitivity, and professional identity. Latent profile analysis was performed using the mean scores of six AI ethical awareness domains. Profile characteristics were compared using chi-square tests and Welch's analysis of variance. Factors associated with profile membership were examined using R3STEP multinomial logistic regression, while differences in professional identity were assessed using the Bolck–Croon–Hagenaars method. Results: Three profiles were identified: consistently low awareness (C1; n = 152, 27.6%), autonomy–education salient (C2; n = 232, 42.2%), and consistently high awareness (C3; n = 166, 30.2%). The three-profile model demonstrated the lowest AIC, BIC, and sample-size-adjusted BIC, with an entropy of 0.876. Educational level, prior AI-related education, AI familiarity, AI tool-use frequency, attitudes towards AI use in nursing, and ethical sensitivity were associated with profile membership in at least one pairwise comparison ( p < 0.05). Attitudes towards AI use in nursing and ethical sensitivity were associated with all three pairwise comparisons. Professional identity scores were lowest in C1 (59.06 ± 7.77), intermediate in C2 (61.15 ± 8.14), and highest in C3 (63.33 ± 7.89). Significant differences were observed across profiles (Wald χ² = 23.739, p < 0.001), with all pairwise comparisons remaining significant after Holm adjustment. Conclusions: A one-size-fits-all approach to AI ethics education may not adequately address nursing interns' diverse learning needs. Nursing educators could consider tailored educational strategies that emphasise critical evaluation of AI-generated information and ethical issues related to transparency, accountability, and algorithmic fairness. Further longitudinal research is warranted to clarify the relationship between AI ethical awareness and professional identity. Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

items.title: Leadership as an AI Governance Capability: A Contingency Model of Effective Human Oversight and Human, AI Complementarity
items.abstract: Assigning a human reviewer to an AI-assisted decision does not ensure meaningful oversight. Reviewers also need the evidence, authority, and time to identify errors and secure appropriate corrections. Building on Ouchen, Chouay, and El Arabi’s (2026) account of leadership as a governance capability, this article develops a contingency model of how those conditions can be established. The model links responsibility boundaries, decision orchestration, and collective learning to three mechanisms: calibrated reliance, actionable contestability, and verified learning feedback. Their expected effects depend on task evaluability, error detectability, review resources, and incentives.

items.title: Learning Companion for students’ critical reasoning and academic writing
items.abstract: The advent of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) transformed technology’s role in the education sector by introducing highly adaptive, interactive tools. Standard implementations are often inadequately designed to effectively aid students. In some cases, these systems hinder genuine learning by inducing cognitive offloading, offering immediate solutions that bypass the cognitive processes necessary for deep conceptual understanding. This concern highlights the need for pedagogically grounded systems that foster genuine understanding and skills development. To address this gap, this paper presents an experimental implementation evaluating the feasibility of embedding formal educational frameworks directly into AI system architecture. We introduce Learning Companion, a prototype engineered to mitigate passive cognitive offloading by translating educational theory into programmatic workflows. Rather than replacing educators or automating learning, the Learning Companion is designed to strengthen meaningful learning interactions by positioning AI as a collaborative partner that supports learner agency through guided dialogue and adaptive instructional scaffolding. Aimed at enhancing critical reasoning and academic writing, the system operationalises Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) through algorithmic Socratic questioning to provide structured instructional scaffolding. This human-centred approach demonstrates how AI can complement teaching and foster deeper learner engagement while preserving meaningful connections between students, educators, and intelligent learning technologies.

items.title: Legal Awareness and Responsible Responses to AI Generated Misinformation in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence can produce convincing misleading text and synthetic media, raising questions about how people assess and respond to online information. This study examines self-reported awareness of possible legal consequences and three distinct responses to potentially false content: considering harm before forwarding, reporting deceptive material and correcting or removing content later found false. It analyses 385 adult, AI-aware questionnaire records from a Bangladesh sample comprising law students, graduates, legal professionals and other respondents. Because the questionnaire does not measure the frequency of exposure to AI misinformation or observed social media activity, the study assesses stated awareness and self-reported practices rather than exposure or actual conduct. Items are analysed separately using descriptive distributions, paired comparisons and exploratory Spearman correlations with Holm adjustment. Legal-consequence awareness was endorsed by 244 respondents (63.4%); consideration of harm by 269 (69.9%); reporting by 268 (69.6%); and correction or removal by 259 (67.3%). Awareness and reporting showed a small positive rank correlation (ρ = .138), whereas the relationships with harm consideration and correction were uncertain after adjustment for three tests. Differences between correlation coefficients require direct comparison; statistical significance in one association alone does not demonstrate a difference across practices. The findings do not show that legal awareness causes responsible behaviour. The article integrates information credibility, media literacy and the theory of planned behaviour as perspectives for a future study with measured exposure, validated items and observed verification tasks.

items.title: Making programming learning visible: Students’ perceptions of an authentic, process-oriented assessment design
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has increased questions about whether a final code artefact alone can constitute sufficient evidence of student learning in programming education. This poster presents a practice-based evaluation of a redesigned second-year programming unit that incorporated multiple forms of evidence of learning. The assessment design is informed by authentic assessment (Boud & Molloy, 2013), feedback for learning (Carless & Boud, 2018) and self-explanation theory (Chi et al., 1989). It responded to current calls for assessment reform in the age of AI by shifting attention from the final artefact to the processes through which students design, explain, test and improve code (Lodge et al., 2023). Across three progressively sequenced assessments, students produced working Python programs, submitted WakaTime development records, recorded video explanations of design decisions, declared and justified GenAI use where permitted, and revisited prior code to improve exception handling and pytest testing. GenAI was allowed under accountable-use conditions, during which students were required to identify GenAI-assisted code, ensure that their submissions used concepts taught in the unit, and demonstrate that they understood and could explain the code they submitted. Assessment 1 established foundational object-oriented programming practices. Assessment 2 asked students to build a weather-data bot using CSV data, web scraping, datetime, logging, collections and pandas analysis. Assessment 3 required students to return to their Assessment 2 codebase and use feedback from Assessment 2 to strengthen its robustness through built-in exceptions, custom exceptions and tests. The design operationalised process-oriented assessment at task level. Code provided product evidence; WakaTime provided process evidence; video explanation provided conceptual evidence; and feedback with staged task design supported iterative development. Together, these tasks created an evidentiary architecture that made programming processes, conceptual reasoning and judgement more visible than final code alone. The evaluation drew on 68 anonymous unit feedback responses. Open-ended feedback was examined using thematic analysis (Clarke & Braun, 2017). Three student-perception themes were emergent. First, authentic tasks positioned programming as professional practice: students valued project-based tasks such as CSV analysis, web scraping and data-processing bots because they resembled meaningful programming work. Second, explanation and process evidence made computational thinking visible: students described shifts from writing code to thinking in terms of modularity, validation, debugging and engineering practice. Third, feedback supported iterative improvement and confidence: students reported that feedback helped them identify errors, revise code and progress more independently. The poster argues that process-oriented programming assessment should not rely only on restricting AI use. Instead, assessment can require multiple forms of evidence to validate student learning (Dawson et al., 2024) such as working code, development traces, self-explanatory video, feedback uptake, accountable AI-use declarations and testing artefacts. Video explanation is especially important because it prompts students to justify programing structures, methods, strategies and data-analysis approaches (Lai & Niblock, 2024). The study is limited by its reliance on one unit, one teaching period and self-reported student feedback. Further analysis of WakaTime data, video explanations, code revisions and pytest artefacts will examine how process evidence relates to conceptual understanding, reasoning and feedback uptake.

items.title: Management Communication in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: Reframing Human Connection, Trust and Leadership Voice in the Algorithmic Workplace
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now drafts memos, summarises meetings, translates messages, analyses employee sentiment and answers customers, placing it at the centre of how managers communicate. This paper examines how these developments are reshaping management communication and what they demand of managers. Using a documented integrative review of 49 sources from management, organisational communication and human–computer interaction, it integrates media richness, sensemaking, sociotechnical systems and organisational trust theories into a multi-level account. A consolidated evidence table and a comparative analysis of seven AI applications show that AI improves the speed, clarity and reach of routine, informational communication, but that messages perceived as heavily AI-written lower judgements of the sender's sincerity, authenticity and trustworthiness, especially for relational and high-stakes messages, and that disclosure alone does not remove this penalty. The paper argues that AI changes the mechanics of management communication more readily than its meaning. It examines the Nigerian context in depth, including infrastructure, linguistic diversity, high power distance and the 2025 data protection directive, together with implementation barriers at technological, organisational, individual, cultural and regulatory levels. It then proposes the Human-Centred AI Communication (HCAIC) framework and positions it against existing frameworks. HCAIC comprises six practices (strategic intent, human oversight, authenticity and transparency, ethical data governance, capability building and employee participation), which act through perceived authenticity, message accuracy and psychological safety to produce trust, clarity and employee voice. Key concepts are operationalised and seven propositions are offered for empirical testing. The paper concludes that the defining managerial competence of the AI era is not generating messages, but making messages mean something to people.

items.title: Managers-as-coaches in digitally mediated work: a practice-based framework for reflective leadership and workplace learning
items.abstract: Purpose This paper examines how reflective judgement is supported through audio-only coaching by managers in digitally mediated work and develops a practice-based framework for reflective leadership and workplace learning, with bounded implications for artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled learning. Design/methodology/approach Practitioner-led, work-applied action research was conducted in a global business-to-business (B2B) sales organisation. The research material comprised contemporaneous written records of fourteen audio-only coaching conversations, participant feedback and reflective journals, as well as approximately one hundred on-the-go records spanning more than one year. Reflexive thematic analysis followed an interpretivist orientation. Findings Four recurring micro-processes were identified: reflective attention, motivational nourishment, value-based reframing and metacognitive regulation. They were most visible when the manager restrained authority, protected silence and left interpretation and action with participants but weakened in urgent exchanges. Audio-only mediation appeared to support openness and listening when combined with relational familiarity, participant preference and protected time. Research limitations/implications The single-organisation design and reliance on contemporaneous written records constrain transferability claims and fine-grained interactional analysis; implications for AI-enabled coaching remain conceptual. Practical implications Managers can use the four micro-processes to preserve reflection and ownership; human resource development (HRD) practitioners can use the framework to design and evaluate digital coaching as workplace learning. Social implications Preserving employees' ownership of judgement may support responsible participation and attention to stakeholder consequences. Originality/value The study integrates four empirically grounded micro-processes into a practice-based framework for reflective workplace learning and offers a bounded, literature-informed bridge between managerial dependency and potential algorithmic conformity.

items.title: Meaningful work in a male-dominated profession: a thematic analysis of women Neapolitan pizza chefs
items.abstract: Purpose This research examined how women pizza chefs construct, negotiate and experience meaningful work within the traditionally male-dominated context of the Neapolitan pizza sector. Design/methodology/approach This study adopted a qualitative research design. Data were collected through 25 semi-structured interviews and analysed using thematic analysis to identify recurring themes and patterns. Findings The findings reveal three interconnected processes through which meaningful work is constructed and negotiated: legitimacy construction, resistance to gender norms and identity transformation. Meaningfulness emerges through ongoing efforts to gain professional recognition, challenge gendered expectations and redefine professional identities within a male-dominated and culturally embedded occupation. Relational dynamics, including customer recognition, mentoring and family support, act as enabling conditions that sustain these processes over time. Originality/value This study highlights how women negotiate their professional identities and define what makes their work meaningful in artisanal and culturally embedded occupations while navigating gendered barriers in hospitality and restaurant contexts.

items.title: Mind the gap: Bridging disconnection in Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL) design
items.abstract: As higher education continues to rapidly digitise with the rise of Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL), the challenge is not only technology implementation or access, but meaningful integration into student-facing learning, assessment, communication and support practices (Chung et al., 2026). Despite increasing investment in TEL, research and practice continues to focus on technology adoption, functionality and efficiency (Feng et al., 2025; Wu & Chen, 2025). Consequently, learning technologies, pedagogy and student services are often treated as separate domains rather than interconnected components of an educational ecosystem (Barrett & Harte, 2023; Børte & Lillejord, 2024). This creates a design problem where students experience fragmentation across systems, processes and support services, leading to disconnection between learning and assessment. Drawing on practice-based evidence and relevant literature, this poster argues that advancing TEL requires intentionally designing connection across the educational ecosystem. This poster employs a practice-based, reflective methodology informed by evidence gathered across two intersecting roles at a research-intensive metropolitan university in Australia. First, as an educational developer involved in learning design, digital assessment implementation, and academic capability development. Second, as a strategic student experience officer within a stakeholder relations team, focused on cross-functional collaboration, service design, stakeholder engagement, and student support. Insights were drawn from implementation observations on digital assessment initiatives, stakeholder interactions across faculties and central service divisions, service-design challenges and student support queries. Recent literature on digital transformation, TEL, student wellbeing, and connected learning ecosystems was used to sensitise and critically inform these reflections, providing a conceptual lens through which patterns and gaps could be identified. This contributed to the development of a conceptual framework that positions learning, support, and technology as interconnected components of a connected educational ecosystem. Insights from the roles highlighted recurring points of disconnection in student facing practices, including assessment processes, support pathways and learning design decisions. These issues emerged at the intersections between academic, professional and technological domains, and were often reinforced by siloed approaches to working. These practice-informed reflections suggest that the future of digital learning depends on the intentional design of connection across students, educators, professional staff, and institutional systems. When learning, assessment, and support are designed in isolation, misalignment and fragmentation can occur, with implications for student success, satisfaction, and motivation (Bull, 2025; Liang et al., 2024). The implications on TEL are to prioritise collaborative connections across student-facing practices. To address the disconnect gap, the poster proposes a “Connection by Design” framework, developed through an iterative process of reflective analysis, stakeholder consultation, and engagement with literature on TEL, student wellbeing, digital transformation and connected learning. Practice-based observations from digital assessment implementation, service design initiatives, stakeholder interactions, support queries, and communication challenges were compared against themes from relevant literature and refined through ongoing professional dialogue, peer feedback, and cross-functional collaboration. This process contributed to the identification of three interdependent dimensions of effective TEL design. The first is human connection, which focuses designing learning and assessment that promote clarity, belonging and productive cognitive engagement (Zhou & Ye, 2024). The second is collaborative connection, which highlights the importance of co-design between academics, education designers and technologists and professional staff. The third is systemic connection, which involves the alignment of digital platforms and services through integration, policy coherence and embedded support pathways. Together, these three dimensions provide a practical approach for diagnosing disconnection and informing more connected, collaborative and human-centred TEL design.

items.title: Miscalibrated AI improves human calibration: An alignment problem for AI-assisted Decision education
items.abstract: Using artificial intelligence (AI) well requires probabilistic thinking, and central to it is calibration: expressing certainty that matches one's actual accuracy. Calibration is a decision skill, but a notoriously difficult one to teach. Because AI systems typically generate a probability alongside every prediction, observing these probabilities may help humans learn to provide better calibrated judgments. This is one form of what we call AI-assisted decision education -- using AI to teach the judgment skills that decision-making requires -- of which learning by observation, as here, is among the simplest forms. In a preregistered experiment, novice participants (N = 300) judged the probability that images of white blood cells were cancerous, before and after exposure to a highly accurate (94%) convolutional neural network. A single model was shown in three ways, holding accuracy fixed while varying the certainty it expressed: its original probabilities, which were conservative and poorly calibrated for the model's accuracy; a recalibrated version, well calibrated for the model and correspondingly certain; or categorical predictions carrying no probability information. When later tested without the AI, only the original, conservative display improved participants' calibration. It did so by reducing over-extremity, without a condition-specific improvement in discrimination. Notably, the display that taught best was the one miscalibrated for the model. AI-assisted decision education therefore faces an alignment problem: the signal that best describes a model, need not be the signal that best supports the learner.

items.title: Mitigating the Negative Consequences of Work Stressors: The Role of Perceived Meaning and Calling
items.abstract: The purpose of the present study was to understand how meaningful work and vocational calling may benefit employees’ work and well-being under circumstances of job stressors. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources framework, we tested a model linking stressor exposure to work and health outcomes through one’s experience of meaningful work, and dependent on one’s perception of work calling via a two time-point survey of 493 employees. Exposure to particular stressors and evaluated workplace and health-relevant outcomes were consistently linked, and further support was found for the role of calling in buffering the impact of certain stressors on outcomes through work meaning. This study contributes to the occupational health and career development literatures by expanding our understanding of detriments to job-related (i.e., job satisfaction and turnover intentions) and well-being-related (i.e., physical symptoms and burnout) criterion variables from workplace stressors. Implications for organizations and counselors, study limitations, and future directions are discussed.

items.title: More than a Second Pair of Eyes: Artificial Intelligence Across the Breast Imaging Pathway
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from stand-alone accuracy studies to prospective deployment across breast screening, risk prediction, multimodal diagnosis, treatment response, and workflow support. The goal of this narrative review is to determine which AI applications have demonstrated clinical benefit, which remain technically promising, and what safeguards are required for implementation. We synthesize randomized trials, prospective cohorts, real-world implementations, external validations, systematic reviews, and guidance identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus through 30 June 2026. In screening, AI-supported mammography can increase cancer detection and reduce reading workload, but effects depend on whether AI is used as concurrent support, an independent reader, triage, or partial autonomy; autonomous workflows may shift work and cost downstream through additional recalls. MASAI met its prespecified noninferiority criterion for interval cancer, but this should not be interpreted as proof of equivalence or mortality benefit. Image-based risk models often discriminate better than density or conventional clinical models, although prospective benefit from AI-guided allocation to supplemental imaging has not yet been demonstrated. Evidence for contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM), MRI, ultrasound, radiomics, and multimodal models is less mature and limited by external validation, domain shift, missing data, operator dependence, and uncertain incremental value beyond clinicopathological factors. Ungrounded large language models and opaque foundation models are not suitable for autonomous clinical advice. Current evidence therefore supports controlled, task-specific integration rather than radiologist replacement; real clinical benefit depends on governance of the whole AI-enabled pathway, including local validation, human factors, downstream resource use, statistical stopping rules, and fallback procedures.

items.title: Negotiating identity and relationality: An AI-enhanced polylogue on human-centred learning design practices
items.abstract: This poster presents a developing AI-enhanced polylogue methodology and conceptual framing to understand how third-space professionals in higher education are negotiating their shifting roles and identities while designing human-centred learning and assessment. Recent technological disruptions (e.g., widespread proliferation, advancement and use of generative AI, focus on cybersecurity, adoption of data-enabled technologies and ecosystems) have intensified tensions around higher education assessment structures and practices, exposing the limitations of isolated, task-based evaluation of student learning (Boud et al., 2020; Corbin et al., 2025). In response to the challenges posed to learning and assessment in the contemporary higher education landscape, emerging scholarship has foregrounded relationality and human connection alongside a shift to more program-wide approaches to assessment and assurance of learning (Lodge et al., 2023; Nicola-Richmond et al., 2025). This has highlighted questions about how educators can sustain meaningful relationships with each other and with students amidst these disruptions (Maldon et al., 2025). In this work-in-progress project, we focus on these relational questions and explore how technological disruptions are reshaping the roles and identities of educators, specifically curriculum designers working in third-space roles at the boundary of academic and professional domains (Whitchurch, 2012). We build on work that positions teaching and learning as fundamentally relational, emphasising connection, trust, care, and dialogue between educators, students, and third-space professionals (Riddle & Hickey, 2023). Our aim is to understand how relationality may be conceptualised in the context of transforming curriculum to support human flourishing and critical engagement with generative AI in our everyday learning design practice, particularly in the design of program-level assessment, feedback, mentorship, and collaborative sense-making structures. The project employs an AI-enhanced polylogue methodology inspired by Markauskaite et al. (2022). The AI-enhanced polylogue is a structured, multi-voiced inquiry, where participants engage in iterative cycles of individual reflection and collaborative dialogue, involving AI as a reflective interlocutor to surface gaps, alternative perspectives, and assumptions. Over several months, three curriculum designers independently responded to targeted questions in reflective logbooks, then engaged in semi-structured conversations about connection in higher education, program-level learning design, evolving educator roles, and the contributions of third-space professionals. This was complemented by a collaborative chat with a generative AI tool, in which participants used AI to probe gaps, tensions, and alternative perspectives arising from the conversations. These strands are then brought together in collaborative critical reflection sessions to identify emerging patterns in relational practice and their significance in program-level curriculum design. This poster shares early themes from the logbooks and conversations. Early analysis highlights how participants experience and navigate tensions between increasing technological mediation alongside their third-space roles and their commitment to relational practice. The importance of human-centred learning design and its implications will also be examined and shared. The project contributes to contemporary discussions on inter-collegial practices that keep connection, trust, and dialogue central in increasingly AI-mediated educational environments. As part of this project, participants treat disruption as an invitation to remake educator identities and practices in more relational, collaborative, and inclusive ways.

items.abstract: Können wir autonomen Fahrzeugen, KI-gestützten Diagnosen oder elektronischen Patientenakten wirklich „vertrauen“? Dieses Kapitel nähert sich dieser Frage aus psychologischer Perspektive und analysiert, was Vertrauen im Umgang mit digitalen Technologien bedeutet. Im Vergleich zwischen menschlicher und technischer Vertrauenswürdigkeit zeigt sich, dass Verlässlichkeit zwar unterschiedlich verstanden wird, aber in beiden Fällen entscheidend für das Gelingen von Interaktion bleibt. Schließlich eröffnet sich die Frage, wie Vertrauen und Misstrauen gegenüber digitalen Systemen gesellschaftliche Dynamiken mitprägen könnten. Das Kapitel lädt dazu ein, Vertrauen nicht als „bloßes Gefühl“, sondern als Schlüssel zur Gestaltung von Mensch-Technik-Interaktion in digitalen Gesellschaften zu begreifen.

items.title: Orchestrate: An AI-secure MarTech simulation for systems thinking and industry-ready capability
items.abstract: Marketing technology (MarTech) education has traditionally emphasised the acquisition of discrete platform skills, often resulting in fragmented, “tool-first” approaches that inadequately prepare graduates to manage complex MarTech ecosystems. At the same time, the rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has intensified concerns about whether conventional assessment designs can validly evaluate higher-order capabilities such as judgement, strategic reasoning, and decision making (Corbin et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2024). These converging challenges highlight an urgent need for Technology Enhanced Learning (TEL) innovations grounded in human-centred design that foster systems thinking and strategic decision making while providing authentic, AI-resilient assessment opportunities. This presentation introduces Orchestrate, a low-fidelity (LoFi) MarTech simulation designed to cultivate systems thinking and assess industry-ready capability development in undergraduate and postgraduate marketing programs. Developed in Microsoft Excel, a widely available and low-barrier technology, the simulation provides a scalable and accessible learning experience. Informed by industry practice, Orchestrate positions students as marketing leaders responsible for managing investments across an interconnected MarTech ecosystem. Piloted during Semester 1, 2026, with Bachelor of Commerce students undertaking the Marketing Technology major at RMIT University, student teams balanced competing priorities to optimise customer acquisition, retention, satisfaction, and revenue growth. Rather than learning isolated technologies, students allocated finite budgets across 12 capability areas aligned to the People, Process, Data, and Technology (PPDT) framework (Monshizada et al., 2023). The pedagogical design is underpinned by systems thinking theory, which emphasises understanding interdependencies, trade-offs, and emergent patterns within complex systems (York et al., 2019). The simulation makes relationships between MarTech capabilities explicit, demonstrating that sustainable organisational performance emerges from balancing people, process, data, and technological priorities rather than investing in individual tools. Authentic assessment principles further situate learning within realistic professional contexts that mirror contemporary marketing practice. A distinctive contribution of Orchestrate lies in its AI-resilient assessment design. Rather than relying on static written outputs that can readily be generated or enhanced by GenAI, assessment focuses on students’ situated decision making within the dynamic simulation environment. Teams must justify their evolving strategies, explain the consequences of their choices, and demonstrate alignment between investment decisions, course principles, and organisational performance outcomes. Because gameplay produces different conditions and outcomes for each team, the design reduces opportunities for inappropriate AI assistance while maintaining a focus on higher-order judgement and strategic reasoning. Early evidence from the Semester 1, 2026 pilot indicates strong student engagement and learning. Assessment submissions demonstrated sustained engagement with the simulation, while reflective responses showed strong understanding of course concepts and application of relevant theoretical frameworks to strategic decisions. Qualitative student experience survey feedback also identified Orchestrate as a key highlight of the course. These findings are indicative rather than the result of a formal research evaluation; a comprehensive Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) study is now being developed, with an ethics application underway, to investigate the simulation’s impact on systems thinking, strategic decision making, student engagement, and learning outcomes.

items.title: Participative leadership and taking charge: feedback-seeking pathways across generations
items.abstract: This study examines how participative leadership promotes employees’ taking charge behavior by focusing on feedback-seeking as a cognitive–behavioral mechanism through which employees manage the responsibility and accountability inherent in change-oriented action. By integrating Social Information Processing and Social Cognitive perspectives, we argue that participative leadership signals shared responsibility and legitimacy for initiative, thereby shaping how employees interpret leadership cues and regulate proactive behavior. Specifically, participative leadership encourages two distinct forms of feedback-seeking—inquiry and monitoring—which differ in visibility, social risk, and informational value. We further propose that generational context conditions how participative leadership cues are interpreted and enacted, resulting in different feedback-seeking responses across generations. Survey data from 350 matched employee–supervisor dyads in South Korea were analyzed using moderated mediation techniques. The results indicate that inquiry mediates the relationship between participative leadership and taking charge, with the indirect effect differing between the categorical generational groups, although the corresponding moderation pattern was not evident when age was modeled continuously. Monitoring did not exhibit a significant mediating effect. These findings suggest that participative leadership fosters proactive behavior through feedback-seeking, while warranting caution in interpreting the inquiry-related group difference as a cohort-specific effect.

items.title: PEDAGOGICAL CONDITIONS FOR USING PHYSICAL ACTIVITY TO SUPPORT PSYCHOLOGICAL WELL-BEING AND DEVELOP PERSONAL STRESS RESILIENCE
items.abstract: The article examines physical activity as a psychological and pedagogical resource for maintaining psychological well-being and developing personal stress resilience. Based on a theoretical analysis and synthesis of findings from contemporary scientific studies, it is established that the psychological potential of physical activity is associated not only with immediate changes in psycho-emotional states but also with the development of an individual’s capacity for emotional self-regulation, conscious behavioral control, mobilization of internal resources, and constructive coping with stressors. Five interrelated psychological and pedagogical mechanisms through which physical activity exerts its influence are systematized: emotional-regulatory, cognitive, motivational-volitional, social-communicative, and adaptive. Their functional significance in maintaining emotional balance, developing cognitive control, strengthening self-efficacy, fostering social support, and enhancing individual adaptive capacities is examined. It is demonstrated that the functioning of these mechanisms depends on individual characteristics, the nature of physical activity, motivational engagement, and the pedagogical conditions under which activities are organized. The pedagogical conditions for using physical activity to maintain psychological well-being and develop stress resilience are identified, including the individualization of physical activity, fostering intrinsic motivation, creating a psychologically safe environment, developing emotional and cognitive self-regulation, promoting reflective engagement, and ensuring the regularity and gradual progression of physical activity sessions. A three-component conceptual model is proposed, integrating pedagogical-organizational, psychological-regulatory, and personal-outcome components and reflecting the functional relationships between the organization of physical activity, the mechanisms of its psychological influence, and the development of personal adaptive resources. It is concluded that the purposeful integration of physical activity into the educational process creates favorable conditions for maintaining psychological well-being, developing stress resilience, and fostering individuals’ capacity for emotional self-regulation, constructive responses to stressors, and adaptation to challenging life circumstances.

items.title: Pengaruh Perceived Organizational Support Dan Self-Efficacy Terhadap Work Engagement Santri Pengelola Unit Usaha Pesantren Al-Mubarok Lanbulan Sampang
items.abstract: Pesantren berkembang sebagai lembaga pendidikan sekaligus pemberdayaan ekonomi melalui unit usaha yang melibatkan santri. Penelitian ini bertujuan menguji hubungan perceived organizational support (POS) dan self-efficacy dengan work engagement santri pengelola unit usaha Pesantren Al-Mubarok Lanbulan Sampang. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan survei non-eksperimental terhadap 84 responden. Analisis meliputi statistik deskriptif, uji normalitas residual, linearitas, heteroskedastisitas, multikolinearitas, dan regresi linear berganda. Hasil menunjukkan bahwa POS berhubungan positif dan signifikan dengan work engagement (B = 0,581; β = 0,485; p < 0,001), demikian pula self-efficacy (B = 0,311; β = 0,215; p = 0,027). Koefisien beta terstandar POS lebih besar daripada self-efficacy, yang menunjukkan hubungan relatif POS lebih kuat dalam model ini. Secara simultan, model signifikan, F(2, 81) = 22,711; p < 0,001, dan menjelaskan 35,9% variasi work engagement (R² = 0,359).. Temuan ini memberikan dukungan awal bagi relevansi job resources dan personal resources dalam menjelaskan work engagement santri yang menjalankan peran sebagai peserta didik sekaligus pengelola unit usaha. Secara praktis, penguatan dukungan pengelola perlu menjadi prioritas yang disertai pengembangan keyakinan kemampuan diri santri pengelola unit usaha.

items.title: People before technology? What do learning designers across sectors see as essential for successful practice?
items.abstract: Positioned at the intersection of pedagogy, technology, and curriculum design, learning designers play an increasingly important role in the design, development, and enhancement of learning experiences across diverse educational contexts. Their work has been described as being characterised by collaboration, relationship-building, and the ability to facilitate change within complex educational environments (Altena et al. 2025; Walji, 2023). Recent research further suggests that effective learning design depends on adaptive relational work, trust, openness, and the integration of diverse forms of expertise across interdisciplinary teams (Papageorgiou & Bennett, 2026). Existing studies have explored learning designers’ demographic profiles, qualifications, professional backgrounds, career pathways, job titles, and professional positioning, particularly within higher education (Altena et al., 2025; Gilmore & Nguyen, 2023; Mitchell et al., 2017; Slade et al., 2019). Learning designers have also been conceptualised as “third-space” or hybrid professionals whose work spans pedagogical, technological, and organisational boundaries (Bennett, 2023; Whitchurch, 2012), and competency frameworks have been proposed to describe their professional capabilities (MacLean & Scott, 2011; Simpson, 2025). However, there remains limited evidence about learning designers working outside higher education and little empirical research examining how learning designers themselves perceive the knowledge, skills, and values that underpin successful professional practice. This presentation reports preliminary findings from a larger survey of 268 learning designers working in Australia (88%) and New Zealand (5%) across diverse contexts, including formal education (K–12 and tertiary), enterprise, government, and not-for-profit organisations. The presentation focuses on respondents’ perceptions of the knowledge, skills, and values that constitute the “special sauce” of learning design practice. Data was collected through a cross-sectional online survey and participation was on a voluntary basis. The findings suggest that learning designers perceive the human-centred dimensions of their work as more central to their professional practice than the technical dimensions commonly associated with the role. Collaboration with subject matter experts was the most frequently reported task performed by learning designers and interpersonal skills were the most frequently selected skill, highlighting the collaborative and relational nature of the role. A high proportion of respondents identified knowledge of learning and motivation theories as a core knowledge domain underpinning effective learning design practice, followed by knowledge of educational technologies and digital learning environments. Strong emphasis was also placed on proficiency with learning management systems as an essential skill. The values identified by respondents further suggest the profession’s strong orientation toward critical thinking, empathy, and adaptability. While technological knowledge and skills were widely recognised as important, particularly educational technology and digital learning environments, and learning management systems, they were identified slightly less frequently than the human-centred aspects of the role. These findings suggest that, although technology is an important component of learning design practice, practitioners primarily appear to prioritise collaboration, learner support, and the application of human judgement as essential to the role rather than technological expertise alone. The presentation concludes by arguing that, as artificial intelligence and automation increasingly undertake routine technical and production tasks, the future value of learning designers may lie less in the technologies they can use and more in their uniquely human capabilities, including empathy, communication, collaboration, critical judgement, and the ability to bring people together around better learning experiences. In this sense, the “special sauce” of learning design practice may not be technological expertise but people skills. Moving the field forward will therefore require a stronger sociological and philosophical foundation for understanding how these human capabilities can be developed, valued, and sustained as educational technologies continue to evolve.

items.title: PONTE: Personalized Orchestration for Natural Language Trustworthy Explanations
items.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) seeks to enhance the transparency and accountability of machine learning systems, yet most methods follow a one-size-fits-all paradigm that neglects user differences in expertise, goals, and cognitive needs. Although Large Language Models can translate technical explanations into natural language, they introduce challenges related to faithfulness and hallucinations. To address these challenges, we present PONTE ( P ersonalized O rchestration for N atural language T rustworthy E xplanations), a human-in-the-loop framework for adaptive and reliable XAI narratives. PONTE models personalization as a closed-loop validation and adaptation process rather than prompt engineering. It combines: (i) a low-dimensional preference model capturing stylistic requirements; (ii) a preference-conditioned generator grounded in structured XAI artifacts; and (iii) verification modules enforcing numerical faithfulness, informational completeness, and stylistic alignment, optionally supported by retrieval-grounded argumentation. User feedback iteratively updates the preference state, enabling quick personalization. Automatic and human evaluations across healthcare and finance domains show that the verification–refinement loop substantially improves completeness and stylistic alignment over validation-free generation. Human studies further confirm strong agreement between intended preference vectors and perceived style, robustness to generation stochasticity, and consistently positive quality assessments.

items.title: Practice-Dependent Development of Discernment: How Doing Can Change What Can Later Be Distinguished
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Practice-Dependent Development of Discernment, an account of how repeated practice with correction can develop a capacity to discriminate that receiving a statement once does not secure. Retained wording, correct performance on practiced cases, and transferable discernment are separate achievements. The account assesses discernment through demonstrated discrimination across specified new cases, with the conditions of practice and feedback recorded. Exposure to a rule, repetition, and success on familiar examples do not alone establish transfer. Statements can accelerate learning and sometimes do much of the work that practice would otherwise do, while repetition without correction can entrench error. The assessment asks what was stated, what was practiced, how errors were corrected, and whether performance transfers under the conditions in which the capacity will be used. The discussion sets the mechanism beside Ericsson, Krampe, and Tesch-Römer’s account of deliberate practice and examines two documented cases. Tanaka, Curran, and Sheinberg’s 2005 bird-identification study compared species-level and family-level training with equal exposure and corrective feedback. The species-level advantage transferred to new photographs of trained species; for entirely new species, it was significant for wading birds but not owls. Accounts of Nainoa Thompson’s training under Mau Piailug and the 1980 voyages of Hōkūle‘a trace the development of wayfinding through corrected practice at sea. Piailug made decisive interventions on the outbound passage. On the return, Thompson made most navigational decisions while his teacher remained aboard but largely kept out of the navigation. Part of the Relational Conditions and Dynamics series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines who arranges practice, supplies correction, defines adequate discernment, and tests transfer. Potential applications in human–AI research include tutoring, training design, and competence assessment that distinguish repeating a rule or succeeding on familiar tasks from discriminating correctly in new cases under specified conditions.

items.title: Productivity Without Prosperity? Who Captures the Economic Gains from Workplace Artificial Intelligence?
items.abstract: Experiments show that generative AI raises productivity on specific tasks by 14 to 40 percent, but who benefits when it spreads through the economy is far less clear. This study builds a capture accounting from task to economy. It links published field and survey evidence on productivity gains, adoption and wage pass-through to an exact decomposition of productivity gains in the U.S. nonfarm business sector, using the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) release of 5 November 2026 and the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey. Between the first quarter of 2024 and the third quarter of 2026, output per hour rose by 6.35 log points; 3.28 points (51.7 percent; rounding interval 50.3 to 53.1) reached workers as higher compensation relative to output prices, and 3.07 points went to nonlabor income as the labor share fell to 53.0 percent, the lowest since 1947. Labor’s capture fell from 84 percent in 2024 to 70 percent in 2025 and turned negative (-16 percent) in the four quarters to 2026 Q3, while nonfinancial corporate unit profits rose 16.1 percent. At the worker level, Danish administrative data show only 3 to 7 percent of productivity gains reaching earnings. A consistency bound combining these pass-through rates with plausible shares of AI in productivity growth implies that AI explains a minority of the rise in nonlabor capture (median 23 percent; 5th to 95th percentile 8 to 38 percent) and cannot be the whole story. The evidence is descriptive and aggregate, and the AI shares are bounds, not estimates. Purpose - This study asks who captures the economic gains from workplace AI, and how much of the recent shift in the distribution of productivity gains could plausibly be attributed to it. Design/methodology/approach - The paper combines published task-level, worker-level and firm-level evidence with an exact capture decomposition of BLS quarterly data, rounding-error Monte Carlo intervals, and a consistency analysis that bounds the AI contribution using pass-through rates and adoption arithmetic. Findings - Roughly half of the recent productivity gain went to workers and half to nonlabor income, with workers’ share falling over time and turning negative in the latest quarters. AI use is concentrated in large firms and in information and finance. Pass-through of AI-specific gains to workers is small, but AI can account for only a minority of the shift. Research limitations/implications - Aggregate indexes are rounded and revised, AI shares of productivity growth are not observed, and field studies are not representative of the economy. The analysis cannot identify causal effects. Practical implications - Bargaining institutions, training and transparency over how time savings are used are likely to determine capture, and policy should track labor’s share of gains alongside productivity. Social implications - Productivity growth need not translate into prosperity for workers, and young entrants in exposed occupations face distinct employment risk. Originality/value - The paper provides a transparent accounting that connects micro and macro evidence on AI’s distributional effects and quantifies what current data can and cannot say.

items.title: Profiles of Generative AI Use and Cognitive Substitution Among Generation Z University Students
items.abstract: University students may use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for practical assistance while delegating independent cognitive activity. We examined whether these behaviors form contrasting profiles or increase together, and whether separate psychological and contextual measures predict profile membership. A cross-sectional survey at a Thai public university yielded 593 analyzed respondents from 634 eligible responses, divided before clustering into development (n = 474) and locked-test (n = 119) cohorts. Two K-means profiles represented lower and higher levels across Information Use, Productivity Use, and Cognitive Substitution; the primary solution did not identify a distinct high-use, low-substitution group. Among development-selected classifiers, the construct-only support vector machine achieved locked-test Macro-F1 of 0.824, compared with 0.787 for combined gradient boosting and 0.553 for context/usage logistic regression. The combined block had the highest development mean Macro-F1 (0.814), but adding context offered little incremental information beyond the constructs. Cognitive Offloading was the strongest predictive discriminator, followed by trust in AI and AI self-efficacy. These associations are conditional on related self-report measures and a sample-specific partition, with substantial disagreement between clustering algorithms. The findings support examining what students delegate alongside usage frequency and motivate assessment that makes independent reasoning visible, without establishing causal mechanisms or learning effects.

items.title: Prompting inclusion: Development of a GenAI prototype to support UDL-aligned course design in computing education
items.abstract: Universal Design for Learning (UDL) offers a valuable framework for developing inclusive and accessible courses, but educators often receive limited support in translating its broad principles into context-specific teaching and assessment practices. This paper reports on the design of a custom generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) conversational assistant prototype developed to support computing educators in Australian tertiary education in applying UDL to their courses. The prototype provides concrete, non-directive suggestions across the three tenets of UDL, multiple means of engagement, representation, action and expression. Rather than treating GenAI as a generic automation tool, the prototype explores how prompt design, scope limitation, structured outputs, and persona-informed contexts can scaffold inclusive pedagogical reflection while maintaining academic judgement. The paper presents the functional prototype as its primary contribution and describes its design considerations, prompt architecture, and early scenario-based testing.
