items.title: Rebalancing the algorithm: A sociotechnical approach
items.abstract: While education shifts further into the digital age, human connection remains irreplaceable. Effective learning is fundamentally a deeply social process, where robust relationships with peers, educators, and communities are indispensable to cognitive, emotional, and ethical development (Noddings, 2013; Vygotsky, 1978). As higher education is increasingly shaped by advanced digital technologies including Generative AI and AI-enabled learning systems, it is essential that educational innovation moves beyond technological capability to consider how advanced technologies can foster human connection, cultivate belonging, support collaboration, and enhance individual and collective wellbeing (Holmes et al., 2019; UNESCO, 2023). This view aligns well with Fink’s (2013) taxonomy of significant learning, which recognises that understanding oneself and others (the human dimension) is a critical component of learning, an integrated process comprising six interrelated dimensions. Cultivating this dimension is vital for developing new values and interests that sustain life-wide and life-long learning, and advance learners’ academic and personal development. With life-wide and life-long learning in mind, we extend Chen’s (2025) learning taxonomy approach that is grounded in Bloom’s (1956) and Fink’s (2013) learning taxonomies to adopt a sociotechnical approach to the design of a postgraduate Information Systems (IS) unit. We designed learning activities and assessments that not only develop disciplinary knowledge and skills required to achieve unit learning outcomes but also empower students to cultivate new values and interests that sustain life-wide and life-long learning. Student feedback and reflection have been positive, suggesting that this approach fosters deep engagement, enhances meaningful learning and increases students’ metacognitive development. We will share key reflections from our teaching practice and invite discussion to explore how sociotechnical approaches can inform the design of AI-enabled IS education to advance life-wide and life-long learning.

items.title: Rebuilding and rehumanising the University of Trust in an era of generative distrust
items.abstract: As higher education institutions accelerate the adoption of generative AI, questions of trust, human agency, and educational purpose are becoming central to the future of technology mediated education. This paper argues that AI has not created a crisis in higher education so much as exposed and accelerated declining trust within teaching, learning, and assessment. Drawing on Humboldt’s conception of the university as a site of productive living tensions, this disciplined provocation examines how technology-mediated education is reshaping the relationships between learners, educators, knowledge, and algorithms. Drawing on inductive theory generated from a two-year constructivist grounded theory study, this paper proposes the notion of epistemic crisis as a way to represent the deficit dialogue driving epistemic change, and the concept of generative distrust exposing the fractures between the productive living tensions that build trust in higher education. The paper contributes to contemporary debates on human-centred learning design by arguing for a rebalancing of the algorithm through pedagogies that foreground care, collegiality, civic engagement, controlled risk and collective mission.

items.title: Reclaiming wonder: Creating meaningful learning experiences in a digital age
items.abstract: The past two decades have seen higher education progressively rely on digital-enabled teaching and learning systems. Learning management systems, lecture recordings, online readings, assessment technologies, and increasingly flexible modes of participation have transformed the student experience (The University of Queensland, 2021, 2025, 2026a, 2026b). In this context, digital technologies have become an essential and expected component of contemporary higher education (The University of Queensland, 2021, 2026a). This Pecha Kucha explores how the rapid evolution of educational technology, culminating with the emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), is prompting educators and students to reconsider questions of authenticity, trust, creativity, and what makes learning memorable, meaningful and distinctly human (Lao et al., 2026; Polyportis, 2023; Rajan & Niranjan, 2025). As GenAI becomes embedded in education, learners are increasingly navigating blurred boundaries between real and generated experiences (Çalli & Alma Çalli, 2025; Lao et al., 2026; Weikmann et al., 2025). Content that once inspired fascination, curiosity, or wonder is increasingly met with scepticism (Çalli & Alma Çalli, 2025; Weikmann et al., 2025). This raises questions about what forms of learning remain uniquely valuable when information, content creation and digital assistance are readily available (Polyportis, 2023; Rajan & Niranjan, 2025). The challenge facing higher education is not whether technology belongs in learning environments, but how it can be meaningfully used to engage students in the learning process. Two examples illustrate this approach. In a humanities literature course, students engaged with the University of Queensland library collections and spaces before developing creative responses to course texts through zines, journals or rewritten scenes. Students could work in paper-based or digital formats, supporting creativity, personal expression and engagement with disciplinary ideas. The resulting exhibition demonstrated diverse interpretations of course concepts and encouraged ownership of learning. In an archaeology course, Gradescope was used to support assessment and feedback processes while learning remained centred on collaborative, in-person activities, creating a tangible “mycelium web” of theory, mapping relationships between concepts into a shared physical artefact. This approach supported collaboration, deeper conceptual understanding and the practical application of theory through active participation. In both examples, technology played a supporting role, enabling greater focus on curiosity, creativity, connection and meaningful learning experiences. While digital technologies have created opportunities for access, flexibility, and inclusion that were previously impossible, educators also have a responsibility to design learning experiences that cultivate curiosity, creativity, human connection, and shared discovery (Rajan & Niranjan, 2025; The University of Queensland, 2021, 2025, 2026a). Yet educators face challenges in selecting appropriate technologies, meeting assessment security requirements, and guiding students in the ethical use of GenAI and the development of human values (Al-Shamaileh et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2025; The University of Queensland, 2026b). Learning designers and other third-space professionals contribute expertise in bringing educators, technologies and human-centred pedagogies together to create engaging learning activities and assessment. Through these examples, attendees will be encouraged to consider how learning environments can foster connection, trust, and engagement in an increasingly AI-mediated world. They will gain practical insights into using technology strategically while preserving the human qualities of learning that foster curiosity, belonging, and participation.

items.title: Reconfiguring Authenticity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Critical Code Analysis of Deepfake Generation and Detection Systems
items.abstract: This study examines how authenticity is constructed and reconfigured within deepfake generation and detection systems. Drawing on the perspective of Science and Technology Studies (STS) and the methodological framework of Critical Technical Practice (CTP), it conducts a critical analysis of the core code of two representative open-source projects, FaceFusion and DeepfakeBench. Through the syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic dimensions of code, the study investigates how authenticity judgments are technically operationalized within deepfake systems. The findings reveal three interrelated processes through which authenticity is reconfigured in deepfake technological systems. First, authenticity undergoes Proxyization, as direct judgment of authenticity itself is increasingly suspended and verisimilitude comes to function as its technological proxy. Second, authenticity undergoes Riskification, as authenticity judgment shifts from factual verification to risk calculation and risk balancing. Third, authenticity undergoes Residualization, as technological systems establish authenticity by continuously identifying and excluding falsity. Consequently, authenticity no longer functions as a positive category requiring direct confirmation. Instead, it becomes a negative category established through the negation of falsity and exists only as the residual state left after falsity has been continuously identified and excluded. More importantly, these processes demonstrate that deepfake technologies are driving a profound transformation of the digital information environment: credibility is increasingly established through the exclusion of falsity rather than the confirmation of truth, thereby reshaping the fundamental logic through which authenticity is established and trust is sustained within the broader social information environment.

items.title: Reframing academic integrity in Australian universities for the Generative AI era
items.abstract: This paper reports initial findings on how the top 10 Australian universities have responded to Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) through their academic integrity policies, guidelines, and AI-related governance documents. Using qualitative policy analysis and thematic analysis of institutional policies and guidelines, this study examines how GenAI use is framed and governed, including how institutional expectations are communicated to students, academics, and administrators. The study also explores how universities frame the opportunities and risks associated with GenAI. The initial findings show a clear shift away from prohibition and surveillance-oriented approaches once common in higher education. Rather than relying on AI detection tools, universities are increasingly emphasising responsible use, transparency, assessment redesign, and shared accountability among students and educators. Academic integrity is being reframed as a matter of learning design and ethical participation rather than solely as compliance and enforcement, moving from a detective to an educative approach. These findings suggest that Australian universities are seeking to balance technological innovation with educational values, offering insights for institutions navigating the evolving relationship between GenAI, assessment, and learning. This paper contributes to ongoing discussions on how higher education can effectively integrate AI while fostering trust, safeguarding academic integrity, and enhancing meaningful learning.

items.title: Revisiting educational foundations for learning in the age of Generative AI
items.abstract: The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has intensified discussions about assessment assurance, academic integrity, and graduate capability in higher education and vocational education and training (VET). Institutional responses have often prioritised assessment security, while a growing body of scholarship has sought to define the competencies required for AI literacy. This position paper argues that these developments, while important, risk overlooking longstanding educational traditions that remain highly relevant in AI-enabled learning environments. Drawing on critical literacy and Students-as-Partners scholarship, we contend that many capabilities now associated with AI literacy reflect enduring concerns regarding critical evaluation, ethical participation, and learner agency. Rather than proposing another AI-specific framework, we argue that established educational traditions provide a robust foundation for helping students engage with AI critically, ethically, and thoughtfully. We conclude by suggesting that educational responses to AI should prioritise critical dialogue and shared responsibility as students prepare for increasingly AI-enabled professional and social contexts.

items.title: Riscos ocupacionais e saúde mental de professores: uma revisão integrativa da literatura
items.abstract: Teaching work is complex and multifaceted, involving demands that go beyond teaching and may favor occupational risks and mental health problems. This study aims to analyze scientific evidence on occupational risks and their repercussions on teachers’ mental health, characterizing the studies, describing their physical and psychological repercussions, verifying differences according to sex or gender, and analyzing coping, prevention, and intervention strategies. Methodologically, this is an integrative literature review, with a search in the Scopus database, from 2021 to 2026, in Portuguese and Spanish, which yielded 36 articles. Original full-text articles on basic education and/or higher education teachers were included, with data related to occupational risks or health problems. Quantitative, observational, and cross-sectional studies predominated. Thematic analysis organized the findings into risk factors, mental and physical repercussions, sociodemographic differences, and protective strategies. The main risk factors were work overload, role conflict and ambiguity, low autonomy, insufficient social support, technostress, work–family conflict, school violence, and career precariousness. The repercussions included burnout, Common Mental Disorders, anxiety, depression, insomnia, psychological distress, musculoskeletal pain, and vocal fatigue. Gender differences were observed, with greater female vulnerability due to the double workday, and variations according to educational level, with emphasis on academic productivism in higher education and postgraduate studies. Protective strategies combined individual resources, collective integrative practices, and institutional and ergonomic measures, although individual resources are insufficient without structural changes. Thus, teacher illness is multidetermined and articulates organizational demands, interpersonal relationships, and individual resources. Mental health promotion requires permanent institutional policies, reduced overload, social support, ergonomic adequacy, and spaces for listening. Finally, longitudinal studies and searches in multiple databases are recommended.

items.title: Scoping review of digital pathology for neoadjuvant rectal cancer response
items.abstract: Aim: Neoadjuvant therapy for locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) yields variable patient responses. Artificial intelligence (AI) and digital pathology offer a novel approach to preoperatively predict treatment outcomes using histomorphological features, potentially guiding organ-preserving strategies. This scoping review maps the current literature on AI-driven neoadjuvant response prediction in LARC to evaluate algorithmic performance and identify methodological gaps. Methods: Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, a structured search of PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library was conducted for studies published within the last 10 years. Studies applying AI algorithms to pretreatment whole-slide images (WSIs) to predict neoadjuvant response in LARC were included. Results: Eleven publications were included. Ten studies used retrospective cohorts only, whereas one study also included a prospective validation cohort of 100 patients. Algorithmic frameworks predominantly featured classical machine learning, using software extraction of predefined features, and deep learning for autonomous pixel analysis. Across heterogeneous endpoints and cohorts, standalone classical machine-learning models reported external validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.811-0.908 (prospective: 0.733), a hybrid microenvironment model reported external AUCs of 0.643-0.656 (prospective: 0.630), and standalone deep-learning models reported an external AUC of 0.723 (internal: 0.710-0.81). Critical limitations across the field include heterogeneous clinical target endpoints, inconsistent baseline staging, and a reliance on “black box” algorithms lacking true biological explainability. Conclusion: AI-driven digital pathology demonstrates strong potential for predicting neoadjuvant treatment response in LARC. However, safe clinical implementation will require standardized endpoints, multimodal integration, and prospective multi-centre validation of algorithms anchored in verifiable tumour biology.

items.title: Skills Intelligence and Skills-Based Organizing: A Bibliometric Mapping of Two Disconnected Literatures (2000–2026)
items.abstract: Skills-based organizing replaces jobs and credentials with information on skills, which artificial intelligence now extracts from job postings, résumés and human resource records at scale. Whether this information is valid for the decisions it supports depends on whether research on skills intelligence and research on human resource management inform each other. We mapped 3649 documents published between 2000 and 2026, screened with a large language model audited against a human reviewer, using co-citation, bibliographic coupling and permutation benchmarks. Managerial and computational research form separate communities: only 13% of coupling links connect them, against 46% expected by chance, and the divide is sharpest between studies of the same practice, recruitment and selection. Computational research, 71% of output in 2023–2025, is itself split between recruitment technology and labor-market analytics; it validates skill information mainly against annotated text, about one study in seven relates it to outcomes, and almost none evaluate the decisions it informs. Taxonomies such as ESCO and O*NET do not bridge the communities; work analysis is the main bridge. We propose a skills intelligence value chain from data to outcomes, with five testable propositions, an audit protocol that translates regulatory requirements into validity evidence for each link, a data schema and mixed-methods design that integrate natural language processing with work analysis, and a research agenda for validating AI-produced skill information.

items.title: Social displacement and relational andragogy in generative artificial intelligence-enhanced learning and teaching
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is changing how students learn and how they seek support. This conceptual paper develops social displacement theory to explain how GenAI may replace interpersonal encounters that would otherwise contribute to social learning, belonging, and access to future support. It proposes the ABCs of Human-GenAI Support Decision-Making, in which (A) achievement, (B) burdens, and (C) connections shape whether students rely on independent effort, human support, GenAI, or a combination of these resources. It then advances relational andragogy as an institutional response suited to connected adult learning in a digital society. Relational andragogy intentionally cultivates trust, compassion, mattering, psychological safety, and mutuality while preserving learner agency. Through these relational conditions, institutions can support achievement over time, respond compassionately to external burdens, strengthen students’ anchors of connection, and develop more informed human-GenAI support choices. The framework does not assume that human support is always preferable or that GenAI use is inherently harmful. Instead, we distinguish augmentative uses that expand access or prepare students for human interaction from substitutive patterns that may progressively weaken learning communities. Practical and theoretical implications are offered for educators, student support services, institutional policy, and future empirical testing.

items.title: Social Interaction Cues and Knowledge Sharing in Generative AI-Enabled Communities: The Mediating Roles of Community Belonging and Peer Recognition
items.abstract: Generative AI-enabled knowledge communities combine machine-generated information with human evaluation, verification, and collaborative refinement. The interpersonal conditions associated with knowledge sharing in these communities remain poorly understood. Drawing on social capital theory, this study examines associations among five social interaction cues, community belonging, peer recognition, and knowledge sharing. Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 585 Tencent ima Knowledge Base users who reported using its community-oriented functions. Structural equation modeling showed that perceived similarity, familiarity, social support, and social interactivity were positively associated with community belonging, whereas familiarity and social interactivity were positively associated with peer recognition. Response synchronicity was not significantly associated with either relational perception. Both relational perceptions were positively associated with self-reported knowledge sharing. Bootstrap analyses identified significant indirect associations through community belonging for similarity, familiarity, social support, and social interactivity, and through peer recognition for familiarity and social interactivity. The findings distinguish community attachment from recognition of individual contributions as relational perceptions associated with knowledge sharing. They extend the contextual application of social capital theory to communities in which AI-assisted content production coexists with interpersonal exchange and may inform practices that support such exchange. The cross-sectional, single-platform design limits causal inference and generalizability beyond the surveyed platform.

items.title: Student use and perceptions of AI: Findings from a 2026 multi-institutional survey
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now a common feature of many students’ study practices, and universities are grappling with its implications for assurance of learning, assessment, academic integrity, effective teaching, student support, and policy. Yet institutional responses are still often shaped by assumptions about student use, capability, trust, integrity, and learning (e.g., Bearman & Fawns, 2024). This project is part of the overall Student Perspectives on AI in Higher Education Project, a four-university collaboration investigating how higher education students in Australia understand and use GenAI in relation to themselves as learners. It included two large scale surveys in 2024 (Chung et al., 2024) and 2026. The 2024 phase of the project showed that GenAI had already become embedded in students’ academic practices, with over 80% of surveyed students in four Australian universities having used it for study-related tasks and nearly half using it regularly (Chung et al., 2026). However, the findings also revealed complex patterns of trust, usefulness, self-directed learning, equity, academic integrity, and pragmatic, task-specific engagement. While this 2024 survey provided an initial snapshot of student engagement with GenAI, the rapid pace of technological and institutional change necessitated a follow-up survey in 2026 for an updated understanding of student practices and experiences. The 2026 survey was adapted from the 2024 instrument and comprised 50 questions and 115 items across demographics, use and usefulness, motivations, assessment and academic integrity, learning and fluency, and perceived impact (Henderson et al., 2026). The survey received 10,222 student responses, with 8,700 students fully completing the survey. The sample included 73% undergraduate students, 75% students aged 18 to 24, 59% women, 29% students who spoke a language other than English at home, 19% first-in-family students, and 24% students who identified as having a disability, health condition, or as neurodivergent. This Pecha Kucha presents descriptive findings from the 2026 survey and, where appropriate, compares these with findings from 2024. The recent 2026 data suggest that student use of AI for study has become more frequent: 20% of students reported daily use and 35% weekly use, compared with 13% daily and 31% weekly in 2024. The most common uses include editing or improving writing, generating ideas or examples, teaching students how to do something, finding information or conducting research, and getting feedback on work. Further, the presentation explores new areas of inquiry introduced in 2026, including AI summarisation of course materials, motivations for using or limiting AI, and AI fluency and learning. Among students who used AI for study, the strongest reasons for use were that it made things faster, helped them get unstuck, made things easier, reduced stress, and increased confidence. The strongest reasons for limiting or avoiding AI included concerns about inaccuracy, personal learning values, wanting to do the work themselves, worry about breaking rules, and ethical concerns. By presenting emerging 2026 findings alongside selected 2024 comparisons, this presentation argues that student voices are essential to developing sustainable, ethical, and educationally meaningful institutional responses to AI in higher education.

items.title: Teacher Metacognitive Scaffolding, Productive and Substitutive Generative AI Offloading, and Self-Regulated Learning in Madrasah Aliyah
items.abstract: Secondary school students increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), and evidence shows it can either support or weaken their self-regulated learning (SRL). This study examined whether teacher metacognitive scaffolding (TMS) and AI literacy (AIL) are related to SRL through productive cognitive offloading (PCO) and substitutive cognitive offloading (SCO), and whether peer collaborative AI use (PCAU) strengthens the link between scaffolding and productive offloading. We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 327 students from 24 classes in eight Indonesian madrasah aliyah (Islamic senior high schools) selected through stratified multistage cluster sampling. We analysed the data using partial least squares structural equation modelling with 10,000 bootstrap subsamples. The measurement model met the reliability and validity criteria. TMS was positively related to PCO (β = 0.378) and negatively related to SCO (β = −0.351), and AIL showed the same pattern with smaller coefficients. PCO was positively related to SRL (β = 0.291), whereas SCO was negatively related to it (β = −0.266). Both forms of offloading partially mediated the relationships of TMS and AIL with SRL. PCAU strengthened the TMS–PCO path (β = 0.257), and scaffolding was not significantly related to productive offloading when peer collaboration was low. The model explained 45.8% of the variance in SRL. The findings indicate that teacher guidance is associated with SRL both directly and, for nearly half of its total effect, through the way students offload their thinking to GenAI, particularly when students verify AI outputs together.

items.title: Teacher–GenAI partnership in design and technology education: From utility to allyship
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping Design and Technology (D&T) education by transforming how design ideas are generated, evaluated, and refined. Although existing research has largely focused on capabilities and limitations of AI, less is known about the emerging teacher–GenAI relationships during authentic design practice. Through semi-structured and recall interviews, classroom observations, reflective journals, design folios and artefacts, this qualitative case study investigated these relationships. Guided by sociomaterial perspectives and using reflexive thematic analysis, the study examined how creativity, agency, knowledge construction, pedagogy, and ethical decision-making emerged through human–GenAI interaction. Findings revealed that pre-service teacher–GenAI partnerships evolved through a developmental trajectory from utility, to dialogue, to teacher orchestration, and ultimately allyship. Rather than functioning as a solution-generating tool, GenAI became a provocateur and generative partner whose educational value emerged through iterative cycles of prompting, critique, reflection, and redesign. The study proposes Orchestrated Co-Agency and the Teacher–GenAI Relationship Continuum as complementary conceptual lenses for understanding these interactions. These lenses could offer new theoretical insights into human–AI co-creation and inform curriculum, pedagogy, and the responsible integration of GenAI in Design and Technology education.

items.title: Teaching beyond AI: Gamified problem-based formative assessment aligned with UNESCO AI competency frameworks
items.abstract: The arrival of capable generative AI (GenAI) tools has posed a genuine and largely unresolved challenge for summative assessment in higher education. When AI-generated submissions evade institutional detection 94% of the time and examination scores rise sharply without any change in teaching, the evidentiary basis of take-home and invigilated assessment is genuinely in question. This paper draws on two lines of work to argue that classroom-based gamified problem-based formative assessment (GPBFA) offers a more durable response than detection-focused approaches. The first line is an empirical study of saval.app, a GPBFA platform evaluated through Keller’s ARCS motivational model across a full university semester (pre n = 41, post n = 44). Results across all four ARCS dimensions were encouraging (all p < .0001; Cronbach’s alpha > .93; composite 81% positive response rate), with near-zero motivational decline across 12 weeks. The second line is a review of UNESCO’s 2024 AI Competency Frameworks for Teachers and Students, which we argue are philosophically and pedagogically aligned with classroom GPBFA in ways the existing literature has not yet made explicit. Taken together, we suggest that moving assessment into the classroom — where it is live, observed, and problem-centred — may address both the integrity challenge and the AI literacy imperative that UNESCO frameworks define.

items.title: THE APPLICATION OF GAMIFICATION IN LITERATURE EDUCATION: IMPROVING STUDENTS' MOTIVATION AND ENGAGEMENT
items.abstract: This article examines the application of gamification in literature education as a means of increasing students' motivation and engagement. It analyses the theoretical foundations of gamification, including self-determination theory and game-based learning principles, and describes a quasi-experimental study in which game elements such as points, levels, badges, quests and narrative roles were integrated into literature lessons. The findings indicate that a carefully designed gamified environment strengthens intrinsic motivation, encourages regular reading, improves participation in discussions and deepens students' interpretation of literary texts.

items.title: The apprenticeship layer: What assessment reform cannot secure on its own
items.abstract: Australian higher education has responded to generative artificial intelligence with an ambitious program of assessment reform. Structural approaches, most visibly the two-lane model, seek to sustain trust in degrees by securing some assessments while opening others to AI partnership. This conceptual paper argues that the reform consensus, now sharpened by sector attention to assurance of learning and adaptive capabilities, addresses validity more directly than formation. Assessment tasks are not only measurement occasions; they can also be sites of the cognitive work through which capability develops. Drawing on cognitive apprenticeship, desirable difficulties and cognitive offloading, the paper introduces the apprenticeship layer: the stratum of entry-level cognitive work through which expertise has historically been developed and renewed. As AI is increasingly used to perform parts of this work in workplaces and universities, institutions face a risk of certifying capabilities without reliably preserving the practice through which those capabilities are formed. The paper proposes three principles for formation-centred design: friction by design, process as both learning and evidence, and a care floor of guaranteed human attention. It concludes that valid judgement and capability formation are different questions that assessment can and should be designed to answer together.

items.title: The Bidirectional Relationship Between XAI and Regulation: Operationalizing XAI for the AI Act
items.abstract: The EU AI Act makes explainability urgent for high-risk AI systems, yet most XAI research focuses on technical metrics rather than regulatory compliance. Understanding how legal requirements reshape XAI method design is challenging: the AI Act regulates organizational obligations without concrete technical requirements, and underrepresents end-users—the very stakeholders whose needs human-centered XAI addresses. As regulations emerge globally, human-centered XAI practitioners face both a challenge and an opportunity: regulations pull XAI research toward real-world deployment, while practitioners can actively shape how explainability enables compliance. This establishes a bidirectional relationship. Our contribution is threefold. First, we provide the first interdisciplinary analysis of XAI’s role in the AI Act—conducted by a team comprising AI Act legal experts, ML engineers, and requirements engineers—on a real-world clinical decision support system. Second, we systematically align XAI stakeholder roles with AI Act legal responsibilities, revealing where explainability methods address regulatory requirements versus where additional measures are necessary. Third, we identify three key insights from which we derive three specific calls to action for human-centered XAI practitioners: actively defining their roles in regulatory implementation; making the user-to-affected-party relationship explicit where regulations address only provider-deployer obligations; and enabling compliance while building multi-level trust—from regulators to affected parties.

items.title: The cost of trust: Human-centred learning design when the process gets fast
items.abstract: Designing an undergraduate systems thinking course in 2023 took months. Workshops, whiteboards, an academic drafting offline, iteration, constructive alignment, compliance, and endless box-moving on a digital canvas. One decision shaped the course: the learning designer judged 10 assessment submission points across 12 weeks excessive and argued to reduce them. The academic, who had taught the discipline for years, refused. Systems thinking concepts interlock, and a student who has not grasped one cannot proceed. The checkpoints were not overload; they were scaffolding. The design bent to the discipline, and the disciplinary expert was right. Generative AI could now compress much of that. It can propose a structure, recommend staggered low-stakes checkpoints for interdependent concepts, and draft the content beneath them. It might well have reached that assessment design faster. Learning designers are tempted to insist something irreplaceable is lost. Much of it is not: a considerable portion of that time was drag, and automating drag is a good outcome. The argument here is not that slowness was valuable. What mattered was less visible. Working on unfamiliar material, the learning designer frequently does not understand the subject. This is usually treated as a limitation. It is better understood as an instrument. The designer is an authentic novice, and their confusion is diagnostic: when an explanation fails for them, it will fail for a student (Wieman, 2007). This is the logic of usability testing: a designer cannot test an interface they already know (Nielsen, 1993). A language model can usefully simulate a novice reader. What it cannot replace is genuine uncertainty: having absorbed the discipline, it fills gaps silently rather than experiencing them. But the instrument only works under a particular social condition. To say “I do not understand this” to an academic, repeatedly, about their own subject, requires standing, which no third space role description confers (Whitchurch, 2008). It is built through months of meetings, shared frustration, and accumulated trust, and it is what made the academic willing to re-explain rather than dismiss. The re-explanation is where the design insight came from. This is the uncomfortable possibility. The inefficiency was not valuable in itself, but the relationship formed inside it, and the relationship is the precondition for the human contribution. Compress the process into an afternoon and the drag disappears, along with the conditions in which trust is made. We have no way to tell which parts of a slow process were waste and which were connection. This Pecha Kucha presents a real course design, concedes what AI could do faster, and identifies what it cannot replace: genuine uncertainty, professional judgement, and trust. For institutions adopting AI-supported workflows, the practical implication is to protect time for co-design and explanation, treating relationship-building as work rather than overhead. It closes with a question beneath the debates about AI and the third space workforce (Bearman et al., 2023; Huijser et al., 2024): if the relationship was produced by the inefficiency we are now eliminating, can human-centred design survive its own optimisation?

items.title: THE MOTIVATIONAL POTENTIAL OF ADAPTIVE PEDAGOGICAL DESIGN IN BLENDED LEARNING FOR HIGHER EDUCATION STUDENTS
items.abstract: This article examines the theoretical foundations of the impact of adaptive pedagogical design in blended learning on the motivation of higher education students. The relevance of this research stems from the digital transformation of higher education, the need to ensure the continuity and quality of the educational process under martial law, and the growing demand for personalised learning tailored to students’ individual abilities, cognitive interests and motivational characteristics. It is emphasised that the effectiveness of blended learning is determined not only by the use of digital platforms and electronic educational resources, but above all by a pedagogically sound combination of classroom and online interaction, flexibility in the organisation of learning activities, and the provision of adequate pedagogical support. The essence of adaptive pedagogical design is explored as a purposeful system for planning, organising and adjusting the educational process, taking into account the individual characteristics of learners. Based on self-determination theory, the importance of satisfying students’ basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence and social interaction in maintaining intrinsic motivation for learning is substantiated. The role of digital educational technologies, learning analytics, personalised feedback and interactive forms of pedagogical interaction in the implementation of an adaptive approach has been identified. The scientific novelty of the study lies in the theoretical justification and systematisation of the pedagogical conditions for implementing an adaptive pedagogical design for blended learning, aimed at maintaining the motivation of higher education students. It is concluded that the comprehensive implementation of the proposed pedagogical conditions creates the prerequisites for enhancing the motivational potential of blended learning and improving its alignment with the individual educational needs of higher education students.

items.title: The promise of Kaospilot: Human connection for programmatic AI review
items.abstract: Generative AI has pushed universities to review curriculum at pace and scale, raising urgent questions about assessment, academic integrity and graduate capability. At Monash University, the Programmatic Assessment and AI Review (PAAIR) project required faculties to examine assessment and AI integration at program level. This paper asks how educational designers can support teaching teams to make program-level curriculum decisions while AI practice, policy and disciplinary expectations are still unsettled. We use a practice-based reflective case study methodology across the faculties of Science, Arts and Information Technology. Data sources include workshop designs, curriculum artefacts, participant feedback, program mapping outputs and facilitator reflection. Our analysis examines how Kaospilot methods, including vision backcasting, shared canvases and visible artefacts, created structured conditions for teaching teams to work with uncertainty, surface disciplinary values and make program-scale thinking visible. The cases show both the promise and constraint of adapting Kaospilot methods to faculty-wide change. The method helped create the human conditions for programmatic AI review, but its impact depended on artefacts, documentation, leadership, governance pathways and continuing educational design work. The paper argues that AI curriculum review requires structured social conditions to enact policy settings.

items.title: The psychological value of creatorship in the era of generative AI
items.abstract: While generative artificial intelligence (AI) can quickly produce appealing work, human involvement in creation may still matter to creators themselves, audiences and those who assign credit. This review examines research across creative, communicative and service domains, including art, literature, music, science, marketing and advice. We organize the evidence by evaluator, by the outcome measured and its timing, and by what was compared, including differences in content, in information about how a work was produced, and in the human role of creation. Outcomes include quality ratings, relational experiences such as feeling heard, and felt ownership. Our framework links specific human activities, such as setting intentions, selecting, revising and verifying, to specific goals. The literature shows that in AI-assisted work, human verification matters for trust in accuracy of the work, their personal input for sincerity, and their choices for the feeling of ownership. The strongest evidence concerns origin-information effects, where labeling the same work as human- versus AI-made can change immediate evaluator ratings. In blinded studies, AI-generated texts were rated higher than human-written texts, yet labeling the text as AI-generated lowered its ratings. These effects vary in size, and sometimes in direction, across contexts and measures. Less is known about the long-term effects of AI-use on creators’ motivation, creative identity, and skills. A well-rated result does not reveal the value of a particular human contribution or the consequences of delegating it to AI. Nor is more human involvement automatically better. Choosing to delegate work or selected work tasks to AI can itself express agency. As AI agents become capable of taking on more creative processes, deciding what to delegate may become a central form of human involvement. This review offers a framework for identifying which contributions matter to whom and for what purpose.

items.title: The Role of Large Language Models in Supply-Chain Decisions: A Systematic Review and Research Agenda
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to supply-chain problems that depend on business documents and natural-language interaction. This review examines how these models support different supply-chain decisions and how they work alongside established analytical methods. Combining bibliometric analysis with a theory, context, characteristics, and methodology (TCCM) synthesis, we examine 81 articles identified through searches covering 40 AJG-ranked operations research and operations management journals, completed in November 2026. In supplier assessment and risk monitoring, LLMs mainly interpret documentary evidence and prepare structured inputs for analysis. In planning, they translate operating requirements into optimization or simulation models and explain the solutions those models compute. In negotiation and replenishment, the generated responses enter the operating choice itself. Most applications rely on prompting coupled with external solvers or evaluators. Alongside these implementations, organisational and analytical studies examine how expected model capabilities shape firm adoption and supply-chain contracts. LLMs therefore tend to complement established decision methods rather than replace them, and both their value and their risks depend on the specific choice they support. We then set five directions: semantic errors in operating decisions, prompts and retrieved histories, explanations and human judgement, information available at the decision date, and shared model development and maintenance.

items.title: The substitute is not the solution: the accountability properties of video-mediated informal knowledge transmission in commercial aviation
items.abstract: Aviation’s informal knowledge channel, through which experienced pilots transmit judgement, technique and professional norms to junior colleagues, is thinning as an experienced cohort retires, and European safety planning identifies this loss as a hazard. This paper examines what is filling the resulting gap. Two corpora of public aviation video were assembled from YouTube by two discovery paths: a browse corpus of 100 high-reach videos from twenty stratified channels and a search corpus of 110 videos returned by twenty-two occupationally framed queries. Both were coded against a common codebook and rated on an identical four-domain instrument, and were never pooled. Technical accuracy was high in both (median 5 of 5), so the concern is not inaccurate content. Contested-event narration, in which speculation can be flagged, evidence weighed and claims anchored to investigative record, occurred on the search path at less than a fifth of its browse-path prevalence (2.8% against 16.7% of coding units), while taught human-factors content persisted. Flagged speculation was absent from the search corpus, and warrants rested largely on personal standing rather than sources. Because genre and discovery path are confounded, this difference may reflect the purpose of instructional material as much as the accountability of its producers. No shared pedagogical standard was observable, and no correction mechanism was identified within the videos; comment-level correction was not analysed. We therefore characterise the pathway as a potential vulnerability rather than an established hazard: competence is conveyed without visibly reproducing the accountability that made workplace informal learning tolerable.

items.title: The tension between artificial intelligence and knowledge: Power relations in the policies of universities and publishing organisations
items.abstract: Maintaining academic integrity is a serious issue in higher education, affecting the paradigms governing the production and dissemination of human knowledge. Although a significant body of research has explored the ethics of AI tool usage in higher education settings, these studies have neglected to examine the power relations inherent within them. In response to this issue, this study employs Bourdieu’s theories of symbolic violence and actor-network theory to review the AI usage policies of Australian higher education institutions and mainstream academic journal publishers. Specifically, actor-network theory is first applied to identify the governance networks surrounding AI usage within the technological adoption process, thereby establishing that AI tools act as mediating agents that actively facilitate communication between institutions and users. Furthermore, symbolic violence provides a comprehensive explanation of the means by which power-holding institutions legitimise such governance. In summary, the aim of this inquiry is to expose and challenge the “false pretences” of AI ethics regulations that merely adjust, reinforce and gloss over the status quo, thereby channelling the potential of AI towards justice and combating latent human bias. items.title: The Trust Calibration Points Framework (TCa-P) - A Revised Theory for Trust Calibration in Automation and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Calibrated trust is considered an important factor for human-system interaction in decision-making. However, definitions of calibrated trust are heterogeneous and research often lacks conceptual clarity. In our work, we conducted a theoretical integration to summarize approaches defining and operationalizing calibrated trust in automation and AI. We then mapped these approaches onto the trust development process that builds on the Trustworthiness Assessment Model (Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025) and the Organizational Trust Model (Mayer et al., 1995). The resulting Trust Calibration Points Framework (TCa-P) offers theoretical clarity and actionable insights for improving trust calibration by identifying six calibration points that can be calibrated to optimize joint human-system performance, and, as a consequence, effective human oversight: maximum joint performance benchmarking, trustworthiness assessment, alignment of individual standards, risk-benefit assessment, dispositions, and behavioral adaptation. The TCa-P emphasizes that trust calibration is not monolithic but instead happens at different points along the trust development process.

items.title: The Trust Calibration Points Framework (TCa-P) - A Revised Theory for Trust Calibration in Automation and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Calibrated trust is considered an important factor for human-system interaction in decision-making. However, definitions of calibrated trust are heterogeneous and research often lacks conceptual clarity. In our work, we conducted a theoretical integration to summarize approaches defining and operationalizing calibrated trust in automation and AI. We then mapped these approaches onto the trust development process that builds on the Trustworthiness Assessment Model (Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025) and the Organizational Trust Model (Mayer et al., 1995). The resulting Trust Calibration Points Framework (TCa-P) offers theoretical clarity and actionable insights for improving trust calibration by identifying six calibration points that can be calibrated to optimize joint human-system performance, and, as a consequence, effective human oversight: maximum joint performance benchmarking, trustworthiness assessment, alignment of individual standards, risk-benefit assessment, dispositions, and behavioral adaptation. The TCa-P emphasizes that trust calibration is not monolithic but instead happens at different points along the trust development process.

items.title: Time to learn? A qualitative interview study on organizational learning time from employee's perspectives
items.abstract: Introduction This qualitative study aimed to examine organizational learning time as a potential measure to facilitate deliberative informal learning within a formally organized frame and to address lack of time as a main barrier to learning. Organizational learning time refers to a fixed amount of time that employers allocate to employees, allowing them to self-directedly, intentionally, and informally engage with work-related topics on a voluntary basis. Methods Because organizational learning time has not yet been systematically studied, we conducted 10 semi-structured interviews with German-speaking employees from various industries. The goal was to explore their attitudes toward a hypothetical introduction of 1 hour of learning time per week within their organization and to identify potential factors influencing its use. We analyzed the data using content-structuring qualitative content analysis, combining deductive categories with inductively developed subcategories. Results Overall, participants had positive attitudes toward organizational learning time and expected both personal development and organizational benefits. Concerns about time in competition with day-to-day business and social acceptance among colleagues emerged as the most frequently mentioned factors influencing anticipated use. Parallels with antecedents of informal learning were identified. Discussion Despite limited generalizability and the intention-behavior gap, the study provides initial insights into anticipated conditions under which organizational learning time might be used successfully. Future research could examine whether it may be particularly useful in organizations where learning is not yet regarded as an integral part of work. While (reactive) informal learning inevitably occurs during work processes, organizational learning time might help organizations to create space for (deliberative) informal learning outside of day-to-day operations. This allows employees to prepare for the rapidly changing demands of the workplace.

items.title: Toward an epistemic ceiling: Collaboration structure, engagement depth, and knowledge activation in an exploratory study of interdisciplinary educator preparation for AI
items.abstract: This exploratory study examines how collaboration structures and engagement processes are associated with interdisciplinary knowledge construction among pre-service professionals engaged in AI-focused instructional design. There is not enough empirical evidence about professional collaboration when designing AI-integrated supports for diverse learners (Martinez-Maldonado et al., 2021; Wan et al., 2021). Little is known about how participation structures relate to the depth of cognitive engagement and knowledge integration that emerges during that process. This study used an exploratory, process-oriented discourse analysis that combined qualitative turn-level coding with descriptive frequencies. The researchers analyzed video-recorded collaborative discourse among pre-service special education teachers and pre-service school psychologists (N = 14) from an interdisciplinary graduate seminar focused on AI-integrated instructional design. The analysis used turn-level coding of participation patterns, cognitive and metacognitive engagement, and activation of an expanded Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework. The expanded framework incorporates Psychological Knowledge (PsychK) and Interdisciplinary Knowledge (IK). The study examined 3111 analytic turns across three interdisciplinary groups. It explored how participation distribution and cross-disciplinary exchange related to epistemic depth during collaboration. Groups with more distributed participation and more cross-disciplinary interaction tended to engage more often in high-level cognitive and metacognitive processes. They also showed broader combined activation of PsychK and IK related to AI tool use, learner variability, and ethical considerations. Groups with more concentrated participation tended toward procedural or discipline-specific reasoning, with limited activation of PsychK and IK. These patterns suggest that collaboration structure may play a role in shaping the kinds of professional knowledge that become salient during AI-focused interdisciplinary work. The study involved three groups in one seminar, its patterns describe these groups and should not be generalized. Group composition by discipline is a plausible alternative explanation for some of them. This exploratory study conceptualized interdisciplinary collaboration as an epistemic practice. It offered empirical insight into how professional knowledge may be negotiated under conditions of AI-mediated educational change. It proposed the epistemic ceiling as an exploratory theoretical proposition for future testing. The findings have implications for interdisciplinary educator preparation programs that aim to support ethical and inclusive AI integration as a collective, relational process. Future research with larger and more diverse samples could examine whether these patterns generalize across institutional and professional contexts.

items.title: Towards human-centred agentic AI mentoring ecosystems for female cybersecurity students
items.abstract: Women remain underrepresented in cybersecurity higher education and the workforce, with participation and retention influenced by confidence, belonging, professional identity, mentoring, and career readiness. While Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly supporting technical learning in cybersecurity, its potential to enhance students’ broader development remains underexplored. This conceptual position paper proposes a Human + Agentic AI mentoring ecosystem in which Agentic AI mentors complement, rather than replace, human mentors, educators, peers, and professional communities. Integrating Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), women in cybersecurity literature, and human-centred AI design, we present a conceptual framework and design implications for Agentic AI mentoring that supports confidence, belonging, professional identity, career readiness and workforce transition. The framework extends AI beyond technical tutoring towards human-centred, co-designed mentoring across academic, social, and professional dimensions.

items.title: TRANSFORMATION OF THE MOTIVATIONAL SPHERE OF HIGHER EDUCATION STUDENTS WITHIN THE SYSTEM OF SUBJECT-SUBJECT INTERACTION
items.abstract: The scientific article investigates the complex problem of the formation and dynamics of motivation in the educational and professional activity of university students within the framework of ongoing educational reforms. The study aims to determine the specific psychological and pedagogical features of students’ learning motives development and to substantiate a system of effective tools, conditions, and factors for increasing their cognitive and professional activity during their university studies. A complex of scientific methods was applied, including a systematic theoretical analysis of psychological literature and an empirical research project (surveying and diagnosing) involving approximately 300 1st, 2nd, and 4th-year students of Vinnytsia Mykhailo Kotsiubynskyi State Pedagogical University, alongside university professors. The findings revealed a highly contradictory dynamics of the motivational sphere across different years of study. While the majority of students maintain a responsible attitude toward their education, the direct cognitive interest, internal learning drive, and emotional satisfaction from the process significantly decrease from junior to senior courses. This drop in intrinsic motivation is gradually replaced by purely pragmatic and formal factors, such as the necessity of passing exams, external attendance control, and future career competitiveness. Based on the results, the key conditions for fostering sustainable intrinsic motivation were highlighted: ensuring intellectual independence, creating problem-based situations, offering a differentiated task system, encouraging freedom of choice, and implementing innovative teaching approaches. The practical value of the work lies in proposing over twenty specific interactive methods to enhance students’ motivational sphere through optimized teacher-student partnership.

items.title: Trust, relationships and impact: Evidencing the human work of learning designers
items.abstract: Learning designers (LDs) play a critical role in supporting higher education teaching and learning, especially through periods of significant digital change, from the rapid transition to online learning during COVID-19 to the redesign of learning and assessment in response to generative AI. In this increasingly digital and AI-enabled higher education sector, learning design is inherently relational, requiring practitioners to meet academics where they are and support educational change through trust, collaboration and compassion. Yet much of this work remains hidden, and difficult to articulate and demonstrate using traditional institutional measures. While output metrics such as consultations, workshops and resources developed provide evidence of activity, they often fail to capture the relational, collaborative and transformative nature of LD practice. Drawing on King and Patterson’s (2026) conception of course design as an act of care, we argue that many of the most significant contributions of LDs are relational rather than transactional. To address this challenge Boreland et al. (2025) developed the Learning Design Evidence Framework (LDEF) which provides a structured approach to evidencing the relational work underpinning educational innovation. The framework makes visible how LDs build trust, foster collaboration, influence practice, and create the conditions for meaningful educational change using seven segments; Student-Centered Design, Curriculum Design and Innovation, Professional Development, Promotion and Sharing of Quality Design, Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, Leadership and Influence, and Recognition and Reward. Across each segment, meaningful impact is demonstrated through collaboration, partnership and sustained engagement with academics, students and institutional stakeholders. Together, the segments provide a structured approach to evidencing the breadth, depth and relational impact of LD practice. This interactive poster invites the ASCILITE community to inform what constitutes meaningful evidence of LD impact, drawing on diverse institutional contexts and practices across the sector. The poster itself is designed to be conversational, inviting delegates to contribute their perspectives by responding to three reflective prompts: What evidence do you think demonstrates the value of relationships and human connection in LD? What contributions of LDs have you noticed are often overlooked or invisible? What evidence do you see as most important in the future? Using pens and markers, or sticky notes, delegates will collectively build a visual representation of the evidence they value, the invisible work they recognise and the future directions they envision for the profession. This participatory approach reflects the framework’s emphasis on co-creation, reflective practice and shared understanding while creating opportunities for meaningful discussion among delegates from diverse institutional contexts. By the conclusion of the conference, the poster will have evolved into a collective representation of how the LD community values evidence, relationships, and impact. In doing so, it will demonstrate that the future of LD is not defined solely by digital technologies, but by the human connections that enable educational transformation.

items.title: Understanding students’ GenAI usage, attitudes, and training needs for equitable and sustainable AI adoption in higher education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is expected to revolutionise Australian’s economy with the potential to generate up to $600 billion per annum to GDP by 2030 (Australian Government, Department of Industry, Science and Resources, 2024). To keep up with the accelerating growth of AI, the higher education sector needs to transition from traditional teaching models to an AI-integrated pedagogy. One of the key concerns in this transition is to ensure equitable and sustainable adoption of AI in higher education. This concern is in line with the UNESCO’s recommendation on the ethics of AI (UNESCO,2021). AI adoption in higher education is both complex and consequential, as it may affect educational ethics through economic disparities among students and heterogenous student attitudes towards task fulfillment (Oxfam, 2022; Vacarelu, 2023). Moreover, it is reframing teaching, learning and assessment design, making it increasing difficult to distinguish between authentic effort, mastery, and output (Mills et al., 2025). Undertaken at an Australian university, this research project aims to addresses two pressing questions in contemporary higher education: how students are currently using generative AI (GenAI) for everyday learning tasks, their attitudes towards it and their AI readiness to support transition towards equitable and sustainable engagement with these tools. By revealing these issues, this project ensures student voices are central to ongoing debates about AI in higher education. Hence, this study is both equity-focused and evidenced-based as it responds to a critical gap for evidence-based insights to inform institutional policy development for a more equitable and sustainable digital ecosystem. Best practice suggests that when policies affecting students are designed with their involvement as co-designers, outcomes significantly improve. Therefore, framed as Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) research, the project places reflective practice and systematic inquiry at the heart of continuous improvement in teaching and learning outcomes. This study uses a quantitative survey method, whereby a structured questionnaire was administered during semester one, 2026. The questionnaire design is based on the Digital Divide and Self-regulated Learning framework. Data were collected from Humanities students across Law, Accounting, Business, and Education disciplines. Results reveal widespread adoption (98%), with some of it uncritical and potentially over-reliant (similar to Palmer, 2023). Notably, outliers exist where students refuse to use the tools entirely. Overall, findings indicate variation in GenAI usage, attitudes, access, and competence, suggesting the need for targeted interventions to advance equitable and sustainable AI integration. The findings are useful as they inform student-centred teaching practices, curriculum design, and policy frameworks aligned with the university’s commitment to innovative, ethical, and inclusive education.

items.title: Unfolding autonomy: the action area of experienced autonomy of individuals in agile project teams
items.abstract: Agile project teams promote autonomy, yet little is known about how individuals actually experience autonomy in their day-to-day work. Building on a multiple-case study of five organisations in a manufacturing context with 61 semi-structured interviews, this study analyzes how individuals experience autonomy in agile project work. Drawing on the critical incident technique, complemented by an associative imagery technique, the paper presents a conceptual model of the action area of experienced autonomy, which unfolds through seven interrelated themes: decision-making, owning, realising, information sharing, learning, supporting, and team organising. The analysis of five cases shows how individuals make sense of this action area, revealing autonomy as a relational, contextual, and situational phenomenon. This study contributes to research on autonomy in management research by advancing the understanding of relational autonomy in agile project teams. It highlights autonomy as an experienced action area rather than a static job design feature or motivational characteristic. For managers structuring agile work in production and engineering environments, the findings offer a diagnostic lens to reflect on and support autonomy, fostering a motivating work context. Methodological contribution is achieved by demonstrating the value of associative imagery in capturing abstract and partly tacit aspects of work experience in agile production and engineering contexts.

items.title: Value-Recontextualizing Decision Support (VRDS) Experiment 2: Cognitive Value Recontextualization and Adaptive Preference Alignment in Human-AI Moral Decision-Making
items.abstract: This preregistration describes Experiment 2 of the Value-Recontextualizing Decision Support (VRDS) project, a PhD study at Florida Institute of Technology. Decision-support systems are usually judged by the quality of the outcome they recommend, rarely by whether a decision fits the decision-maker's own values. VRDS treats a choice that goes against a person's earlier values as a signal worth examining. It uses two mechanisms. Cognitive Value Recontextualization (CVR) shows such a choice from another point of view: a different framing of the situation, and a person affected by the choice. Adaptive Preference Alignment (APA) asks the person to clarify their priorities before the system updates its picture of their values. In the project's first experiment (N = 52), the full CVR+APA condition gave the highest value consistency without a measurable loss in performance. This experiment tests whether that holds in a larger sample and across several moral domains. Design. An online, between-subjects experiment with four conditions in a 2 × 2 design (CVR present or absent × APA present or absent): CVR+APA, CVR only, APA only, and Baseline (neither mechanism). The server assigns each participant to the condition with the fewest participants so far, so the four conditions stay balanced. All participants first answer four short blocks that measure their values. They then make choices in six moral scenarios: a chemical-leak evacuation, a wildfire evacuation, a limited cancer-treatment allocation, cuts to home-care visits inside an employer's rules, the same cuts decided by someone else, and a city repair rule chosen behind a veil of ignorance. Finally they see a summary of their own choices and answer feedback questions. The study takes at least 35 minutes. Participants. 104 adults recruited and paid through Prolific (26 per condition), plus students of one artificial intelligence course at Florida Tech who may take part for course credit (about 50). Hypotheses and expected outcomes. 23 hypotheses in four families, each with one primary hypothesis. (A) Conditions: participants in CVR+APA will make choices more consistent with their own values (Value Consistency Index, VCI) than participants in Baseline. (B) Position: how far a choice departs from a person's values will differ between deciding the care-visit cuts inside an employer's rules and receiving the same cuts decided by someone else. (C) Prediction: the system's Moral Prediction Function will predict the rule each participant chooses behind the veil of ignorance, before seeing the prediction, more often than chance (25%). (D) Performance: when a first pick goes against the participant's values and a reflection, clarification or confirmation step follows, the final choice will perform equivalently to the first choice (within ±5 points on a 0-100 scale). The four primary hypotheses are Holm-corrected together.

items.title: Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments
items.abstract: As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance---which we implement in Gandalf, an open-source verifier. Finally, we evaluate Gandalf against three existing verifiers on BVB. Gandalf matches or exceeds every baseline's F1 at lower cost: with Gemini 3 Flash it matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost, and with GPT-5.4 models it improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost. Gandalf also generalizes to OpenClaw, a structurally different personal-productivity environment, where it again achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934 for the best baseline). We release BVB, Gandalf, and the code and data to reproduce our experiments.

items.title: WATERFALL: Workflow for Adaptive Training with Evolutionary Reward Formulation and Automated Learning Loops
items.abstract: Reward design remains a central bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in sparse-reward, long-horizon and partially observable settings requiring dependency chaining, memory, and deceptive affordance disambiguation. While recent foundation-model approaches reduce manual reward engineering, most assume goal-conditioning, task descriptions, expert demonstrations, or ground-truth metrics. These assumptions are problematic in partially observable environments, where task-relevant objectives, affordances, and dynamics must be discovered through interaction rather than disclosed a priori. We formalise this problem setting by introducing WATERFALL, an iterative population-based workflow for automated reward discovery under the strict observability constraints inherent in POMDP environments. WATERFALL achieves this by (i) synthesising diverse programmatic reward candidates via persona-conditioned generation, (ii) evaluating candidate behaviour from raw visual rollouts utilising a Swiss-system evolutionary tournament judged by vision-language models to identify elites, and (iii) leveraging longitudinal assessment histories to iteratively mutate, escalate, or prune candidates. We evaluate WATERFALL across fully observable and reveal-gated partially observable environments ranging from discrete to continuous, comparing against sparse-reward RL, intrinsic-motivation and foundation-model reward-synthesis baselines. Our results indicate that WATERFALL discovers and refines reward programs without access to privileged information, outperforming baselines that retain their native information advantages, most clearly in the POMDP regime. Extensive ablations substantiate that visual evidence, tournament-based selection, and iterative refinement are jointly important. Enforcing this contract is what separates autonomous reward discovery from benchmark-privileged reward shaping.

items.title: What AI can and cannot do: A cognitive-depth framework for differentiated AI integration in higher education
items.abstract: Higher education has responded to generative AI largely by regulating it by task, specifying where the technology may or may not be used in each assessment. This paper argues that task-based regulation uses the wrong unit of analysis. A single task typically spans several types of cognitive work, and a tool that can be welcomed for one type may quietly displace another. This conceptual paper proposes a four-level framework of cognitive engagement, adapted from classical Chinese expressions about knowing and articulated in contemporary cognitive terms: broad knowledge acquisition, analogical transfer, contextual inference, and original creation. The levels are ordered along a single axis, from cognitive work that is codifiable and reducible to rules and patterns, to work that is situated and dependent on human judgement. This axis maps closely onto the boundary of what generative AI can and cannot do: capability is near-complete at the codifiable end and degrades sharply as work becomes situated. The framework thus functions as a diagnostic lens for design, allowing educators to assign AI a role matched to the cognitive work a task is meant to develop. Two illustrative cases show the framework guiding differentiated, defensible decisions about AI integration within a single assessment.

items.title: What holds and what breaks: Boundary objects in AI-enabled curriculum governance
items.abstract: Universities govern AI adoption through artefacts. Policies, rubrics, assessment briefs, vendor evaluation frameworks, and design templates cross organisational boundaries and carry meaning differently in each context. This paper applies the concept of boundary objects within a cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) framework to analyse which artefacts effectively mediate AI governance across academic, institutional, and commercial activity systems, and which fail. Drawing on the author’s framework for negotiated legitimacy in interacting activity systems and reflexive practitioner experience as an education design leader, the paper develops a typology of AI governance boundary objects classified by origin, interpretive flexibility, and failure mode. The analysis identifies three structural conditions that determine whether a boundary object supports or undermines the legitimacy of learning designers who broker AI adoption across systems. These are co-design across activity systems, support for transformation rather than coordination alone, and resistance to capture by a single system’s logic. It also identifies a failure dynamic specific to generative AI, in which an unstable referent causes artefacts to decay. The paper offers practical design principles for governance artefacts and connects them to a wider question, namely how institutions keep human and pedagogical judgement central as they adopt digital technologies.

items.title: What makes AI educational? A sociocultural framework for transforming AI from artefact to mediating tool
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet much of its use positions AI as a private productivity tool for generating answers, feedback or text. This paper argues that AI is not educational simply because it produces outputs. From a sociocultural perspective, its educational significance emerges when pedagogical design transforms it from an artefact into a mediating tool for participation in disciplinary learning. The paper introduces the AI Mediated Participation Framework, grounded in mediated learning, appropriation and participation. It proposes three design principles: preserving learner ownership, scaffolding thinking through dialogue, and developing AI literacy through disciplinary practice. These principles operate through questioning, dialogue, reflection, critical evaluation and decision making to support learner agency, evaluative judgement, responsible AI use, critical thinking and knowledge construction. The framework is illustrated through AI learning activities in undergraduate and postgraduate educational research courses, where educator modelling, peer discussion and disciplinary expectations repositioned AI from a private feedback service to a mediating tool for methodological reasoning and researcher judgement. The framework shifts attention from what AI can do to how pedagogical design determines what AI becomes educationally.
